I thoroughly enjoyed this book, and give it four and a half stars very enthusiastic stars. Oh what the heck... let's round it up to five. Yeah, it's really good, and not a "typical" ghost story at all. 
 Yeah, one of the characters is a ghost... but she isn't exactly scary. A little pushy maybe. And smelly. Yeah, she's definitely smelly. Then again, during her life as a pirate, she didn't exactly smell like lilacs and roses, and another couple hundred years without a bath haven't helped a bit. 
 When Graciela leaves her cheating ex-fiance behind, and moves across the country to South Carolina to take care of her ailing grandfather, she hopes returning to the safe cocoon of his love will help her get her life back together again, and hopes to heal some broken relationships from her past, and to regain her lost self-confidence and adventurous spirit, too. Well, she got a lot of what she was looking for... especially the adventurous spirit part, although not precisely in the way she expected. She never expected the "adventurous spirit" to turn out to be a long-dead pirate named Anne Bonnie. Never expected to become friends with that smelly ghost, either. Or with the new hunky mayor in town. 
 This book touches on so many different topics... like life, death, friendship, love, hatred, and forgiveness. Parts of it made me cry, parts of it made me laugh out loud, and parts of it scared me just a teensy little bit. (Not the pirate ghost... something else.) Let's just say it has a little bit of everything... and it's all good. Although this book could stand on its own, it is the first in a series, a series which I can't wait to read. I've already bought the second book.

Ilona Andrews is by far the best author I have ever had the pleasure to come across. Every single book Andrews has written has captivated me completely. Someone who doesn't know me would think I would be acting over the top about this, but I truly feel blessed that we have Gordan and Ilona. Their characters are real, and vibrant. Their command of their readers hearts is flawless. Their books always carry the perfect amount of humor at just the right times. I truly treasure their work. 
 Please excuse my gushing, I feel this review is towards all of their works as a whole. So I should really be talking about this one book. I get a little carried away when I think about Ilona Andrews' books. 
 One Fell Sweep was amazing! I will confess I read most of this book while I should have been working, but there was no way I was going to be able to get anything done while I knew an Ilona Andrews book sat unread. There was never a dull moment, never a time where the story dragged. I love every moment of this book, my only complaint being that it had to end. 
 I cried. At work. 
 Andrews knows just what heart strings to tug on. Without spoilers, I will say that I loved how everyone had their own interaction with her after the seed. Everyone had their small moment that meant so so much, the each showed they cared in a way that made perfect since to their character. The universe Andrews has created is so real, not everything is beautiful, not everything is alien and strange. It has such a amazing a balance, and oh the Mystery!(yes, with a capital 'M') We get so much information about this universe, and are craving more. The possibilities are endless. I cannot help but hope this series gets as many, if not more, books than their Kate Daniels series! (The only issue I see with that is being able to think up so many more sweep related titles! haha!)

The fantastic Oscar nominated movie Lion is based on this true story. It is the tale of an impoverished and malnourished Indian boy who got lost at a train station, gets on a train, and is transported to Calcutta 1000 miles from his home. He spends a harrowing month on the streets, lands in an orphanage, and is adopted by a white couple in Tasmania. Fast forward 25 years: the boy turned man exhaustively searches for his home, using google earth, and finds it. 
 If the story was not true one would say the plot was just too improbable. The author does a phenomenal job of depicting what it must have been like for that little boy before and after he got lost. I actually felt hungry when he described searching for discarded morsels of food. I also loved the drama of his internet search. The movie is better than the book (Hollywood vs a Tasmania 30-year-old) but I still read it in one sitting. Six star if that was an option.

Betty White is a big deal because she's charming, fun, still working, brassy and very likable. This memoir is much the same. I listened to it on audio and thoroughly enjoyed her reading to me. She tells little stories about her more recent work ventures like Hot in Cleveland, love interests, aging, working in television, her love of animals . . . in short, all the things you want to hear from her. I enjoyed her candor, humor and obvious joy in what she does. I like that she can laugh at herself as well as at the world. If you're a fan of her or just a fan of TV, you might enjoy the book as much as I did. --CF

Vampires, humans and magic...Oh my! 
 Sunset is a fascinating look at a world that includes Sentinels, Daywalkers and Nightwalkers, metahuman races that have existed for centuries alongside humans without the humans knowing about their existence. 
 Until a terrorist known as Medusa tries to destroy Los Angeles. 
 The world in this story is brought to life with complex and intricate detail. A lot of thought was put into the characteristics of each metahuman group and how these groups function both as individual groups as well as allies. 
 A lot of the set up and worldbuilding is done in flashback/flashforward sequences from different characters' perspectives at different times in their lives. In the beginning, I was confused by the different POVs but I gradually figured out the flow of the book and was drawn into the story. It was a good way for me to get to know each of the major characters. 
 Because there is so much detail involved, the start of the book can be daunting to some readers as there is much to learn about the groups and the characters in each group. At times, there's a feeling of being overloaded with information. I felt this most keenly when Nicholas met with the President of the United States. Nevertheless, understanding the concepts in this book is necessary and the story picks up once most of the worldbuilding is out of the way. 
 One of my favorite characters is Jeremy. In fact, I was rather upset when he suddenly disappeared early on in the book when I expected him to play a larger role. He becomes an important character later in the book but his reappearance felt very sudden since he disappeared early on and the development of his relationship with Nick seemed to come out of nowhere. Nonetheless, I was very pleased to see him play a more crucial role in the story. That scene where Nick's primal mating instinct turned Nick into an enraged jealous vampire over Jeremy was exciting to read. 
 Nick didn't interest me much at the start of the book, but I grew to like him more as the story progressed. I was quite amused to see many love interests for Nick and he's so oblivious to them! I just couldn't get the image of Nick being a juicy bone that the hungry dogs were fighting over out of my head. 
 There's a lot of juicy intrigue and political maneuvering to whet my interest. Some of the methods to resolving certain problems (e.g. Nick's Paris problem and Lorcan's issues with the Fifth Council) were amusingly expeditious. 
 A thrilling tale and I even shed a few tears at the end.

I remember reading this book when I was about 12 & being totally engrossed by this crazy cat world. Heck, they even had their very own language - I'm not too embarassed to admit, I tried to use it in real conversations (hey, I was 12!) 
 This story enchanted me - I've re-read it about 5 times - and I do beleive it's what first turned me on to the fantasy genre. 
 I think I need to read it again soon.

Cannot begin to tell how much I enjoyed this book and how much I learned about a book that is about to celebrate its 75th anniversary. I truly do not believe that there has been another book that has generated so much international interest before, during, after, and even 75 years later. 
 If anyone has any interest in Mitchell's GONE WITH THE WIND, then they must read this book. If you have ever read GWTW, then you need to read this book. 
 I learned so much and enjoyed every page.

Combines teenage preoccupation with the significance of physical beauty, and the secret suspicion that unattractiveness has an intrinsic morality about it to form the backbone of a pretty stirring story of post-apocalyptic adolescent love and rebellion. Of its shortcomings I will say the science of the science fiction is typically perfunctory. Similarly, a perhaps too-complex question about medical ethics that pops up near the end is reduced to a mere plot twist for engendering further adventures.
As the series draws to its inevitable conclusion, exciting things happen in here. This manga has enough drama and suspense, but not overmuch, and this volume should not disappoint.

This book. What to even say? 
 This was my second time reading it, and what struck me most was the idea of how the smallest actions can have huge, life-altering results. The domino scene at the Steiners' home was a particularly beautiful, concrete image of that theme. 
 While I like that the novel allows room for interpretation on sorrow and why we suffer, I do think the last line was pretty weak. I wanted some kind of definitive statement about life, other than just wonder. 
 That being said, I think the novel is absolutely enchanting and would highly recommend it.

Diamond Willow lives in a remote part of Alaska - in a place where you need sled dogs to get to your grandparents' house and if your brother wants to come home from university, he has to fly back home since there are no working roads in the winter. 
 She is shy but passionately loves the sled dogs that she cares for with her Dad and spends more time with the dogs than she does with anyone else at her middle school. 
 When she and the sled dogs ride home from her Athabascan grandparents' home, she and the lead dog, Roxy, take a blind curve too fast and both she and the dog, Roxy, are injured. Roxy is injured so severely that Willow's parents consider putting her to sleep because a blind sled dog is of no use to anyone. 
 This frustrates Willow so much that she takes off with Roxy into a snowstorm. 
 Once Willow and Roxy are recovered, the whole family has a heart-to-heart, and Willow learns long-held secrets. 
 The story is written in a series of diamond-shaped poems with darker *secret* sections in the middle of each poem that indicate Willow's unconscious thoughts. Interspersed with these poems are the thoughts of her ancestors - giving insight as to Willow's family history as well as how these ancestors, reincarnated as animals, are actually watching over their descendants. 
 While I really liked the story, I longed for the defter touch of Louise Erdrich. I feel like Erdrich has told this type of story before and better, but I loved that Frost made the effort.

Young-adult poetry - nai-tochnoto opredelenie za tazi stikhosbirka. 
 Mnogo kharesakh samata knizhka - belotata na stranitsite, razpolozhenieto na stikhovete, razbiraemiia ezik i skromnite iliustratsii. 
 Istinata e, obache, che niakak po-mezhdu drugoto gi prochetokh stikhovete - bez da sgrabchvat vnimanieto mi i da ne go puskat; bez da me pleniat i ostaviat opustoshena; bez da usetia avtorkata da se prokradva v moeto s'znanie chrez napisanite dumi. Tova me nat'zhi. 
 Stikhovete sami po sebe si mi kharesakha, no ne namerikha otzvuk v men. Stoiakh i si se chudekh zashcho taka se poluchi i se prokradna mis'lta, che mozhe bi e zashchoto otdavna minakh tazi v'zrast, v koiato opisanite neshcha sa imali znachenie za men, ili zashchoto moite godini na mlad v'zrasten ne se prepokrivat kato useshchaniia s neinite. Koeto i ot dvete da e, mi dade khrana za razmis'l, koeto me nakara da priema toplo i polozhitelno stikhosbirkata. 
 Chetem knigi, za da namerim sebe si i dori, kogato ne uspeem, to tova s'shcho oznachava neshcho. ^^
This is an absolutely amazing story! It really shows you how lucky we are to feel emotions and have the freedom of choice.

Colin Pearce, the Earl of Ivorwood is in love. He has been for the past year and half. The lady of his affection is his neighbor, Josie Cardworthy. They had grew up together, were great friends. But the night he realized his love, Colin's best friend Captain Nicholas Hargrave had caught Josie's eye. 3 months later, they are engaged. Nick was called to duty and later declared dead. What is a man like Colin to do, when he still is in love with Josie? Specially when Josie and her spinster sister Edwinia are sent to London for the Season. The story continues as the Season gets more intense with love interest for Edwinia and the jealous feelings Josie begins to develope for Colin. What happens when Nick returns unexpected? This book is a good read with twist and turns for each sister to find true love. The home life of Josie and Edwinia with their mother is laugh out loud funny. I found MISCHIEF BY MOONLIGHT to be a light, fun, humorous true romance.

This novel was a lovely adventure set in a windswept village where people hide in their homes from an ancient man-eating serpent. The local minister is frustrated by the hysteria, while recently widowed Cora arrives from the city to search out the monster. Various storylines sprout from these two characters. Divided into four sections, and then again by calendar months, the story presents various characters, all likeable and sympathetic. My favourite part of the book was the setting, but I did find the story dragged on unnecessarily, which kept me wondering if I'd already read that section because parts felt repetitive and predictable. I would recommend this novel to lovers of the classics, I did enjoy it.

Abso-freaking-lutely amazing. Go figure why it took me 8 months to read this. I don't even know why. I'd loved the first book and I guess delay after delay, I forgot about it entirely. A grave mistake because this is a swoon-worthy sequel that had me hyperventilating from page one to page. 
 In case you're not familiar with the plot, then let me hook you up. Some years before, a disease that targets children spread. Some died but some didn't. Those who didn't die have powers. The government with the excuse of rehabilitation took those children from their parents and kept them in special facilities in order to keep them under control. 
 In the first book, Ruby, as sixteen-year-old girl wanders about after breaking out from Thurmond (a rehabilitation facility) when she meets some kids from the League of Children, an organization leaded by a former politician, who wants to take down the current governor of the United States. Ruby is an Orange, meaning she can get inside people's head, see their memories, take control of them. In the first book she's not able to control her powers all that well which is why when she touches the hand of a member of the League of Children, she sees his memory of killing two children mercilessly because he thought they were worthless. She then runs away and comes across, Liam, Chubs and Zu and thus the adventure begins. 
 Ruby has evolved so much in the sequel, it's impossible to think of her as that fragile, broken little girl she was when all of this began. Now, she's working with the League, and runs ops for them. But something is brewing inside the League, someone is trying to take control and do as they please with those they deem worthless. With the help of Jude and Vida, fellow LoC members, she must retrieve the lost usb stick that Liam's brother, Cole, lost. Liam is unaware of the existence of such a stick sewn inside the jacket, which he took from his last visit home, and was his brothers. So, that means Ruby has to search for Liam. 
 "I feel like I'm losing my damn mind, like your face has been carved into my heart, and I don't remember when, and I don't understand why, but the scar is there, and I can't get it to heal. It won't go. I can't make it fade. And you won't even look at me." 
 Hence the name of fhe book: Never Fade 
 Don't worry, there's lot of Chubs in this, I love the guy too. I promise you, you're going to love the new characters. Jude is really young and he's so protective it's kind of cute. Vida, well she's badass, and "bitch" is her favorite word, but you're gonna warm up to her. 
 There are lots of twists, lots of unpredictable moments, and a cliffhanger in the end which accounts for an omg moment. Alexandra Bracken, despite her age, she's pretty brilliant when it comes to describing military procedures and writing amazing, action-packed scenes. 
 If you liked the first book, then I don't doubt that you'll like this as much. In my case, I loved the first book and loved this book even more, because of the character development, and evolution of the world, that's been taken to a whole new level.

I had a hard time rating this one because at times I thought it was going to be four stars and yet it didn't hold me until the end. (I was the last in my "buddy read" to finish.) Maybe my expectations were too high, as I was 
 really 
 looking forward to Tru & Pen's story. 
 The thing that bugged me the most was that, in order to enjoy it -- because it was certainly "well written" with plenty of action and love scenes -- was that I had to pretty much shrug and say, "Oh, well!" to the lack of character continuity from one book to the next. 
 Loved 
 Mason in the first book; though he was a macho kickass a$$hat, he changed b/c of love. Yet I felt the authors tried to keep his character type throughout the series, with only glimpses of the original heroes' personalities (Chris & Tru), instead of going with the great foundations that they already had for these two!! So therefore it was formulaic. That and a couple of set ups that switched agendas... 
 Still, I liked Pen... and was glad to see their HEA.

This book was amazing, as most David Levithan books are. It takes place all in one night and you really follow the range of emotions of the main characters. They are intense and romantic and sexual and passionate and independent and confident and uncertain. I liked the telling from two points of view and I liked the incorporation of so much music. I knew a lot of it, but now I want to go listen to the rest.

I couldn't stop myself from writing a gushing review for the first book in the Collector series, and I'm going to have to do it again for The Barrier Between! I jumped right into this book, having been thoroughly hooked by The City in Embers, and only a few days later have finished, now thirsting for the 3rd book (for which I have to wait a whole 3 months! Across the Divide releases Dec 9th. Yes it's already on my calendar in BIG letters). 
 In this book, Zoey and Ryker find a small respite in their flee for their lives (from various fae, gangs and government officials) during which time they have to figure out what to do about the whole Zoey having Ryker's powers thing. Somehow that is the less stressful thing in their lives at the moment. The tension between the two during this phase ramps way up. That is not to say they don't still regularly butt heads, but they are beginning to respect each other, overcome their biases against each other's species, and finally notice that they are sexually attracted to each other. Some very hot scenes! Stacey Marie Brown keeps the characters true to their nature while letting them evolve, and she writes some amazing, non-cliche romance thrown in with all her creative, heart-pounding storyline. There is intensity in their emotions, the action, and the plot twists.These kinks--the appearance of people and places from the beginning of their adventure--thrown into the little family life that Ryker, Zoey and their hilarious child-like monkey-sprite Sprig have created definitely spice up the conflict (and sexual tension) and escalate the intrigue before causing me to smack face-first into another breath-halting, frustrating (though I must respect the author's ability to get me to that level of attachment) cliffhanger. 
 I am very impressed that the story did not falter or lose intensity as the romance stepped up, and once again loved the quick pace, detailed descriptions and flowing writing style of Stacey Marie Brown. Prepare to become part of the collector world and all the danger and emotion that entails with this book; the best word I can use to describe The Barrier Between is "intense." I am literally counting down the days til I can reenter the Collector world and see how Zoey will get out of her new predicament and whether she will get the few simple things she wants: her monkey BFF, the guy, freedom, his life and her own life. Nothing too extravagant. I'm sure it'll be a piece of honey-cake.
It's nice to see Harley stand up to Mistah J for once.

Part of the 2016 Reading Challenge: A book that's becoming a movie this year 
 I read this book a long time ago, probably in elementary school, but it was so long ago that it was like reading it for the first time all over again. 
 It's a charming book that has fun with its fantasy elements, and it feels like it's being told through the eyes of a child. It could be a little hard to understand at times (especially in the beginning with the BFG), which did make it drag a little, but it was a fairly easy story to follow along with. I can see how it would be an enjoyable book for young kids, but it didn't have enough tension to really keep my interest.

Fetch is about a dog named Fetch that has the courage to leave what is "normal" and soar to great heights in an airplane and discover what lies in a distant world. I loved this book and I think young children will love it also. It teaches children about faithfulness, loyalty and undying love. The love between a child and his dog. The full-page illustrations are simply amazing and will draw any child's attention and keep them engaged in the story. It's a short story but beautifully done and small children will want to read it again and again. I recommend this book very highly to anyone with a small child 
 Disclaimer: I received a complimentary copy of this book from the publisher for my honest review and no monetary compensation was received.

 This . . . This book series has completely overthrown me. I'm in book hangover. T.L. Smith is a brilliant author. Though I own a few of her books, I haven't had a chance to pick one up until this series. I'm in love. T.L. Smith's writing has flow, depth, intrigue and captivates you. Grab your copy now!

This book offers insight into how Jonathan experiences life as he watches his father, Dr. Harry Kozol, deal with his Alzheimer's disease. Dr. Kozol spent his life as a neurologist and in the early stages is able to explain his sickness as his dementia progresses. 
 The books shows vulnerability of the author as he tries to make sense of the memories that have left an impact on his life over the years. In a particular passage, his mother references the 'penalty of love' that a caregiver experiences when they have to look after another individual. For anyone who has been in those shoes, they know the road is not easy. 
 I enjoyed the book. More about my personal review can be found on: http://hesaidbooksorme.blogspot.com. 
 Disclaimer: I was awarded this book in a Goodreads giveaway. While I did not pay for the book, the opinions expressed in this book review are strictly my own.

Another quirky collection by Edward Gorey. Again we have the wonderful pen and ink drawing combined with the droll dark humour Gorey is known for. 
 The book consists of a selection of Limericks about various people in mostly dreary ominous situations. Some of these include throwing children at ceilings, murder, suicide and bathing in brine. Delightful. I can imagine this was quite controversial in 1954. 
 As before these tales of dark humour will not amuse everyone. I think several are animated shorts waiting to happen. They would look amazing animated classically in the same pen and ink styles as the original drawings.
I really wanted to like this more and I tend to enjoy dark books but this is a bit too dark for me. there were parts so hard to read I was cringing.

After I finished this one, I went back and changed the first book's rating to five stars. Why? Because the only thing that bothered me was the undercover/drug ring theme that felt relatively stupid. In the second book though, I got used to it, looked past it and it grew on me. I ended up liking the first one even more. 
 Durbin could have been a really great teacher if he wasn't, you know, such a creep. I didn't doubt him at first even after Janie was suspicious because I didn't think this part would be revealed this early. I was wrong. This was a much more interesting case than the drug ring of the last book though. 
 Now, WHERE is her mom? I mean seriously! I don't remember her having any lines during this book. I'm trying really hard not to judge her as a terrible mother because everyone has his/her own story. But seriously where the hell is she?! 
 I think 
 I love this dream curse too much to let anything else in the book bother me 
 though. And that it actually has a price. It's somewhat feasible you know? It's not just that it sucks to have it like other YA books. It actually has serious problems that you cannot easily get over. I mean blindness? I can't even imagine! Losing function in her hands? Like being blind isn't enough. 
 Cabel is hot and cold. On and off. He always has good reasons I guess but he goes about them the wrong way. 
 Thankfully Janie is not whiney. And the few occasions she was, she recognized the signs and stopped herself. I mean you can't help but whine sometimes, it's just the way it is. But it's also important not to be such a drama queen 24/7.

He writes of rattlesnakes, all kinds of birds, water, women, and place and a seeming fondness for gods that touch his life in these places. Well worth reading because he asks us to look at the familiar with a different set of eyes.

"Because I love you.' It was easy to say it this time now that I understood what it meant. Then I quoted his own words back to him. 'Not just when it's easy. All the time." 
 For a minute there I think my heart stopped. 
 I've had my bad share of series-finale books. Some got left me sad, some left me disappointed, and some even left me incredibly ticked off. So I was wary while reading Horde. I was wishfully thinking this would not blow up in my face. Thankfully, Ann Aguirre did not fail me. Oh! Thank you, Ms. Aguirre for such a wonderful ending! 
 I hadn't put a lot of thought to this series when I first started off with Enclave. To me, it felt like another one of those zombie stories, blah, blah and blah. But then when I met Deuce and Fade, they poked my interest over what kind of story these characters would be going through. And so I fell in love with these two, and over time, as I watch them grow I couldn't bear to think of these two apart. 
 Deuce has always been a strong character from the start. But it was humbling to see a sensitive side of her.  Zen Master Poems by Dick Allen is a lovely collection of modern Zen poetry that brings the essence of Zen into the everyday world. These poems, written in a variety of styles, speak to one on so many levels. They flow beautifully, and will make you stop, to ponder and process, which is what any good poetry should do, but doubly so for Zen poetry. You'll be left yearning for a simpler life, against the crush of the frenetic pace of daily existence. 
 Allen's poems invite one to pause and contemplate the quieter side of the coin, and the fullness of the One Which All and Nothing. I loved the imagery evoked through his words. To Be with a Koan equates existence with lemonade powder dissolving in water, being stirred by something other than one's self, until eventually there is only you, and nothing stirs. How Good It Would Be entices one to think about how peaceful life would if only we could cease questioning things. 
 How Can I Keep Them Together was a personal favourite. It's all about the question of keeping a child's sense of wonder into one's adult years. Words Collected was another favourite. It's a list poem of colours and materials that reveals itself to be a meditation niche. Moment was a beautiful example of mindfulness in action, focusing on the simple act of opening a jam jar. 
 These are just a few of the offerings within Allen's Zen Master Poems. Each and every one is a jewel to be treasured.

101. THE THIEF TAKER, BY C. S. QUINN 
 This is a bit of a mixed recommendation. The person who recommended it did so with the words "read it so we can discuss how awful it was afterwards". It has to be said, though, that she's a History researcher who specializes in 17th century (1600s) England. 
 Synopsis: Charlie Tuesday is a thief-taker, something like a 17th century private investigator. His business is dwindling with the outburst of plague that threatens to empty the entire city -- both because of people fleeing and because of people dying. A beautiful woman offers him lots of money to investigate her sister's death, and Charlie is compelled to accept her offer, but once he sees the body he realizes the crime might have much deeper connections with his own life. 
 Overall enjoyment: I actually liked it, to the despair of my friend. I'm no historian (although I do appreciate well-done research) so the historical inaccuracies didn't really bother me, I only cared about the story's development. That is not to say it didn't have problems; it did, and many, but for a first novel I thought it was a very good effort. I'll definitely read the next one (I just found out today that it is a series...) 
 Plot: There is some nice suspense, and it mostly holds true through the end. I'd say it's probably a lot more thriller than historical fiction. The story kept me turning pages until it was done. It could have been better foreshadowed, there were some inconsistencies, and sometimes the motivations aren't very clear, but overall, it's good enough. 
 Characters: Charlie is interesting, and nicely developed. Maria needs A LOT more work, though. And the other characters, nobility and commoners, are quite shallow and a bit stereotypical. The main problem here were the inconsistencies, but I'm hoping there will be less of those in future books. 
 World/setting: Here, I'm going to have to heed my friend's words and give the book a negative mark. Apparently, the history is all over the place. And so is the geography. I always get suspicious of historical fiction books that don't have a "historical note" in the end, detailing the author's research, what liberties they took, what is historical fact, what was adapted, and what was downright made up. This book doesn't have one, and, according to my friend, for good reason. Even when you don't take history in consideration, there are still many inconsistencies: they are so afraid of the plague at first, but after a few chapters they will walk in plague-infested streets without taking any precaution, stuff like that. 
 Writing style: Pleasant enough, I suppose, although it could have been more fluid. One thing that really bothered me was how she built the romance between Charlie and Maria... Namely, there are several instances when Charlie smells her perfume, or her hair. Dude, you've been on the road for days. You haven't bathed since. In fact, it's the 1600s in Europe, so the both of you probably haven't bathed in months. Are you seriously trying to tell me she smells good? 
 Representation: Not very good. 
 Political correctness: It's kind of the standard thriller. The girl is only there to serve as support and love interest to the male character. She may be smart, but she's also stupid enough to provide them with timely obstacles whenever the story needs it. She's brave, but she doesn't miss an opportunity to shake in fear and cling to him fetchingly (and give him a nice whiff of her perfume in the process). She's so stereotyped she's even supposed to smell good under the circumstances she's in. 
 Up next: City of the Beasts, by Isabel Allende

The Indie world keeps throwing up newer and newer surprises to what I read. This book was a prime example of that. 
 The blurb reads, 
 "Obsessed with Vaush and the desire to protect his realm, Comron embarks on a thrilling odyssey that plunges them into the midst of epic battles and political power struggles, all while being relentlessly pursued by those seeking to control or kill Vaush" 
 To tell you the truth, I read the first line,

 And then I started. And that is where I was taken aback.

It really reminded me of the adage that there is always something soft inside a man who is gruff.

2013 was the year of board game resurgence. With a plethora of options for online, multiplayer, mobile phone, and persistent video games, it might seem that board games would go the way of film negatives. But you can't really banter over Words with Friends--well, I suppose you could. But I don't. Most of the enjoyment of video games hangs completely on their characteristics; their presentation, their mechanics. Board games, on the other hand, are almost entirely dependent on the company you keep to make the experience enjoyable. And so it is with The Republic of Thieves--the characters are strong enough to make a mildly pedestrian plot palatable. 
 Structurally, I adored this, the third book in The Gentleman Bastards series. The caveat here is that, after seeing that there was a third in the series, I went to pick up the second--Red Seas Under Red Skies and, holding it in my hands, made it all the way to the checkout counter before the backcover blurb jogged enough of my memory to recall that I had already read it. So, again, the whole series is more about the characters than what they are doing at any given time; the plot of the first and second books have congealed in my mind into one large mass; sort of like trying to remember which Rocky movie has Mr. T in it. One of them. I know Apollo Creed is from, what, One and Three? Ivan Drago is in Four? Or Three and Four. Whatever, does it really matter? After all, they're all pretty good. If you're not into Rocky, outline the differences in the Die Hards. It is not easy. 
 Back to structure. I'm pretty confident talking about the events of the prior books, since this is a review of the third in the series--anyway, most of the merry band of protagonists have bit it by this point. Not in A Song of Ice & Fire "shocking spectacle" style, but in casual, "Hey man, the RNG says that was a critical hit from a lightning bolt. Sorry brother," sort of fashion. If I've lost you on RNG, it's "random number generator" which, in the case of most board games that rely on chance, are dice. Some video games have an RNG, too. But unlike a video game that has one or more digital win/lose paradigms, board games don't simply end because your character or faction or corporation is hit with a setback (or a lightning bolt).There's no "Game Over" screen for straying from the plot, or invisible walls that funnel you into developer-sanctioned portions of the world. You want to barter your Monopoly money into having someone else pay for drinks, or trade Reading Railroad for a week's worth of doing the dishes? Nobody's stopping you. Simply try playing the electronic version of Apples to Apples against the computer, where certain cards are always programmed to win. Learn those cards, win every time. You lose the entire "ridiculous justification of your answer" portion of the game and begin to recognize that while they are all "games," board- and videogames often have little functional overlap. 
 Digression completed; board games are about the people playing them. But wait! Wouldn't that make a book more like a video game, where you are hemmed in by the words the author has chosen to select, much like you are controlled by the world the game designers and programmers have created? Well, no--because your agency in a video game is usually delimited by the very structure of the thing--and in a book, your agency isn't even on the table. And, I'll remind you, I never compared books to either board- or videogames. What I said was " the characters [of this book] are strong enough to make a mildly pedestrian plot palatable." In distinguishing board- and videogames from each other the demarcation lies somewhere between the freeform, restrictionless nature of employing a set of arbitrary rules upon tokens or cards that symbolize an abstraction of some concept and letting a group of people have at them, versus a predefined, digitally enforced "win or lose" paradigm that can and often does close off access to continuing. There are times you simply cannot proceed in a videogame if you don't play by the rules. That doesn't happen in a board game, because the players can simply alter rules on the fly. You're hemmed in by nothing other than--if you'll permit me this cliche--your imagination. So, the ubiquity of digital entertainment is not an issue of supplanting board games, but of differentiation in their inherent structure, regardless of them both being games. How this relates to books, and this book in particular? While the plot of The Republic of Thieves--plot being the driving force of most fiction--can become a bit bogged down with fluff, the characters and how they do what they do, rather than just what they do, remains appealing. Think about how you might find playing a game of cribbage--certainly not very glamorous--with your friends more exciting than playing Call of Duty--huge explosions! High production values!--with strangers. 
 Anyway, structure of the book, yes, I'm getting there. So we're in the third book, right? And most of the "good" guys have died off. How, then, do you return to pretty great characters whose literary lives were far too short--"False names are fun," said Calo "Call me Beefwit Smallcock." 
 "These are aliases, not biographical sketches," said Galdo.--while still advancing the overarching narrative? Parallel, timeshifted contemporaneous plots, that's how! One plot is set in the past--let us call it Plotline A--which ostensibly exists to inform and expand the current timeline--Plotline One--with backstory and foreshadowing but functionally creates a playground in which to have new adventures with old characters. It's very effective. 
 Both storylines could be their own books. Honestly, they both have their own separate yet tangential narrative arcs, and both pay off pretty well. The infamous point-of-view switching of contemporary fantasy--the one that leaves you dreading Sansa chapters ending just to reveal another tedious Bran whinefest--is alleviated almost completely. Never did I want to skip one timeline in favor of returning to the "good" one, because they were both strong in their own right and interwoven well enough to flow seamlessly between themselves. Really, my only complaint about The Republic of Thieves was that having two full plots rolled into one book created a sense of bloat near the end of the "major" storyline. By the time Plotline One wrapped up, Plotline A had already thrilled and delighted--it had the familiar, likable characters, remember? In fact, with only about one-hundred-and-fifty pages to go--typically the "event horizon" milestone that flings me heedlessly into a book's ending at breakneck speed--I found myself beginning to weary of the actionless meanderings of the Plotline One. Even the title, The Republic Of Thieves, directly references Plotline A. The main timeline serves mostly to reset the world, leaving Locke and Jean idling in a neutral position for the next novel. Functionally. 
 That's not to say it isn't fun, because it is. For the most part. It just doesn't seem to do much of anything. The big reveal at the end isn't gasp-worthy--in fact, it's more of a series of little twists than anything else. For a heist book, it's a bit anticlimactic. I never marveled at the character's foresight or was wowed by their ingenuity. But then again, there are two concurrent plotlines going off at once. And they both did have their own payoffs. So you're getting a lot more excitement than most books, just spread throughout the six-hundred-some-odd pages. And there is a sort of meta-reveal, a hint at the through-thread of the series' major plotline that touches on the mysterious nature of the main character himself. Yet that felt superfluous to me, kind of an also-ran that did nothing and means nothing for the nature of this particular narrative. I dunno, maybe that's just me. I suppose if you count the metanarrative of the entire series, you're getting three climaxes. And perhaps Plotline A and Plotline One are relying on the sort of, "Luke, I amyour Father" moment to pack the emotional, gasp-wrenching twist. But this is not a Dark Middle Chapter, and Locke simply isn't Luke. He's Han. And while everyone knows Han is the best and true protagonist of the original Star Wars Trilogy, no one gives a flip about who his father is. 
 The Republic of Thieves is a reminder that good fiction can have the fun, open nature of a board game. Great characters that were removed in prior books returned to the narrative with panache rather than hackneyed, soap-opera exceptionalism. The series as a whole is one of the most enjoyable to read in modern Fantasy, and after seeing that the author is capable of maintaining appealing characters while creating a more intricate structural format, I remain on board for the next book. I can only hope that the group-heist style prevails over the auspicious rumblings of the prototypical Fantasy-novel-main-character-singular-destiny-Campbellian-heroic-journey that seems to be on the horizon.

 I recently subscribed to Hearts Collective and when you subscribe you have the opportunity to read and review their latest novels when they come out (so people go subscribe!!). So I got an email saying that Impulsively was out and that, if I wished, I could get a copy to review it, you just had to email Hearts Collective. 
 They answered really quick so after about half an hour I was in the possession of this book. 
 I was super excited to start reading this because I am HUGE fan of biker books so I've read my fare share and that's probably why I'm so picky and hard to satisfy. There are biker books out there who rock and those who plainly suck! 
 Impulsively was somewhere in the middle. 
 I think that if I would've read this book before all those other biker books then I may have given it 4 or maybe even 5 stars but since I didn't I'm gonna stick with three. 
 For me, Impulsively can be divided in two parts, a spongebob part and a patrick part (yes, I know this is weird, a spongebob and patrick part what??? I saw this gif and thought it expressed my feelings perfectly so work with me here, pretend that this is all completely normal) 
 SP (from the beginning until about 60%) and a PP (from about 60% until the ending). 
 SP 
 Like I said before, until about 60% of the book the story was fantastic, 4/5 stars worthy. 
 The author had me constantly guessing. I had all these kind of different theories on how things would progress and she kept me on the tip of my chair, turning pages like a madman. I was literally jumping around every time one of my theories proved to be right. 
 I was also very impressed and pleasantly surprised when the author didn't go with the cliche way when a big secret is revealed, which is: secret is revealed, big fight, they break up but eventually get back together. 
 No the author did the logical thing, she let Brooks and Red talk it out like the adults they are. 
 I would have probably smashed my iPad otherwise. 
 Speaking of Brooks, I know the exact moment when he won me over 
 "We've already checked her out, Dec," Kelly adds. 
 "She's perfect." 
 "Damn right," 
 He only had to say those two words and bam I was sold! Later he says stuff like this 
 "You may have never been with a real man before, but you're nothing if not a real woman. We were built for each other, babe." 
 I'm just kidding, I'm not cut out to be an old lady and Red and Brooks are build for each other so honestly, I don't stand a chance. 
 Now unfortunately we've come to the PP of the review. 
 The SP was fast paced and the PP was kinda boring at times. 
 I feel like the author just said to herself fuck logic and because of that I was kinda getting annoyed and frustrated so normally I would rate this book 2 stars but since the first 60% was fantastic I gave it 3. 
 Especially Quinn was often getting on my nerves, the way she handled things, the way she reacted to certain events, it really bothered me. For example she's losing her faith in the FBI. She says that she changed her way of thinking but honestly she didn't. She may have changed her mind and realized that not all MC's are criminals but her way of thinking is exactly the same. 
 She joined the FBI because of one horrible incident that made her want to put the bad guys behind bars. This is totally reasonable but she also left the FBI because of one horrible incident. Was she so naive that she thought that the FBI only consists of good guys? Did she realize the FBI was not her thing and did she want a way out? I honestly don't know and frankly don't care. 
 Then there is Bruno, a character that I found really inconsistent. Bruno is portrayed as this huge scary guy who is corrupt. Someone who for years has been putting bad guys behind bars in favor of other bad guys and nobody has ever noticed it. But then in the end he gets played by Quinn, she records his confession and when he finds she did that out he gets scared. umm what??? I'm sorry but I find it hard to believe that he would be fooled so quickly. I mean he has to be a pretty smart guy, I don't think everybody can just fool the FBI for years. So I found the way how Bruno got arrested and everything pretty hard to believe. There is more but I'm gonna keep it at that. These 2 are the 2 most annoying and frustrating parts of all. 
 Not to be completalty negative about Quinn. I envisioned her as the female version of Eric Beal (only people who watch NCIS: Los Angeles will understand this and I find this pretty kick ass. 
 Overall it was an okay read. I think I may check out the her other books. thanks again to Hearts Collective and of course Colleen Masters!

 This is by far my favorite edition of Paradise Lost. Since the text is full of archaic references, understanding what is meant can often be difficult (and result in a lot of trips to reference books). 
 But this edition provides footnotes that explain each reference and allusion, making reading much easier (and understandable). 
 Also included are a couple other smaller works by Milton, as well as thoughts and criticism on Paradise Lost (most notably the contribution from C.S. Lewis).

The Keeper: Christmas in Salem is an anthology with stories from four authors. I don't normally do anthologies because I just don't get into them but since this one was a paranormal Christmas read I decided to give it a try. 
 Do You Fear What I Fear by Heather Graham 
 This story opens with this darkness moving in on Salem. It started gradually but now it is Christmas Eve and there is verily any daylight left. Nobody has a clue where the darkness is coming from and it's up to the Keepers to find out what it is. Samantha is Keeper of the Vampires and she doesn't think it is something that the vamps could do but she still has to make sure. She is also in charge of her families traditional Christmas Eve party. Daniel is a vampire that Samantha was in love with and then he left. It was seen as taboo for the keeper and a vampire to be together and she told him to go, but she hoped he would stay. Now he is back because he was sent by the council and Sam sees it as the council not thinking she can do things on her own. Can Daniel convince Sam that he came back for her? 
 The Fright Before Christmas by Deborah LeBlanc 
 Rebecca is Keeper of the Five Elements and Sam has asked her for help finding out what the darkness is, so it starts off with a meeting of the elements. When Quieten shows up late it is because one of his black holes has gone missing. If they don't find Teezee it could disrupt the universal balance. Vaughn was the other person whom Rebecca had to beat in order to become the KOTE, but she also had a crush on him. He left abruptly after they kissed one night and he hasn't shown back up till now. She is not happy to see him but she also knows she needs his help in finding Teezee. Vaughn is back to try and win Rebecca's heart and he hopes it isn't to late. 
 Unholy Night by Kathleen Pickering 
 Katie Sue is the Keeper of the Selkie and is also in love with one of them, Jett. They don't get to see each other much since he only sheds his Selkie skin for a few days before he goes back into the water for seven years at a time. It's not the best thing for a relationship, but he could give up being a Selkie and take on a human form forever. It's something not to be taken lightly and he believes it is what killed his mother. While they are absorbed in each other inside a sleeping bag on the beach someone steals Jett's coat. If he doesn't get it back he is trapped on land forever. Jett knows it is a shapeshifter who has stolen his coat and it's a race against time to find it before the shapeshifter destroys it to make potions. 
 Leo the shapeshifter is infatuated with Katie Sue and wants her for himself. He stole the coat to make himself more powerful so he can break away from his master. His master has something to do with the darkness that has fallen on Salem and even though that doesn't bother him he just wants to be free of his master and make Katie Sue his. 
 Strange things happen and Katie Sue and Jett will have a lot to decide. 
 Stalking in a Winter Wonderland by Beth Ciotta 
 The keepers are starting to figure out where the darkness is coming from and now it's up to June, Keeper of the Witches. June feels bad because she hasn't been paying close attention to her job as keeper. She just got word that her uncle died making her the new keeper and she had to move back to Salem. Salem brings up a lot of bad memories for her, one of those is Baz. Eight years ago she found out that she had been under a love spell and that her and Baz were not really in love. Hurt she took off to do research on witches and wiccans and all their rituals, but now she is back. Now she has to work with Baz to try and track down a wizard who is responsible for the darkness and being so close to him brings up a lot of bad memories as well as good. Baz knows that she was hurt, but he didn't have anything to do with the spell and things were really a lot of misunderstandings. Baz has always been in love with June if she would just give him another chance. 
 June has an idea to bring the people of Salem together and help break the darkness spell. Defeat the negativity with good will after all it is Christmas. It takes all the keepers and those in the community to band together to shed some light on their Christmas day. 
 The Keepers: Christmas in Salem is an anthology that takes a main storyline of The Darkness and then spins it over four different stories written by four different authors. Each author took a a keeper and spun a story around them and included the darkness with the last story finding an end to the darkness. 
 All the stories were okay in their own right and there was a little repetitiveness, but I don't see how they could do the four stories without some bits of rehashing from the other stories. I have only read one of these authors prior to reading this and I thought each story was okay, but I think it is much to hard for to put four stories into one sort of main story. I think I prefer anthologies to have separate stories that don't have anything to do with the other except be from the same genre. 
 Overall I will say that it was an okay holiday read and if you like paranormal anthologies you might like it.

The Club Dumas is a very detailed (at times, too detailed) thriller telling the story of a mercenary book collector/detective that is hired to find the three remaining copies of "The Nine Doors", an ancient book that the reader is led to believe could be written by the devil himself. 
 There is an A and B plot line that makes the adventure a fun read. The seemingly unrelated story lines are brought together fairly well at the end of the novel. 
 The Club Dumas is rich with atmosphere and adventure and the author does a rather nice job of drawing some parallels between the protagonist and his friends and the characters of "The Three Muskateers", which happens to be one of the books that makes up one of the plot lines. 
 Overall the book was pretty good, but I found there to be an overabundance of historical details at times, or maybe it's just the way the reader is narrated those details. 
 Ironically, I did not know there was a movie based on this book and it just so happened to be starting on TV at precisely the time I was finishing the book. The book is much better than the movie (usually goes without saying). 
 I would recommend the book to folks that are interested in literature as there are some great references to many great authors. 
 By the way, the movie was so bad that I'm wondering if I didn't take a star off my rating of the novel simply because I can't get the terrible movie out of my head.

This is a fast-paced expose of political and cultural intrigue in fifteenth century Moorish Spain. Thomas Berrington, an Englishman renowned for his surgical skills, has been gifted a wounded concubine, Helena, by the Sultan. Thomas is ambivalent but you don't say no to the Sultan. Life for Thomas is brutal and earthy. He treats battle injuries and witnesses a beheading before going on to the public baths to answer the Sultan's summons. When the Sultan asks him to investigate a series of attacks on women in the palace, he can't refuse. Thomas is supported in his investigative endeavour by Jorge, one of the palace eunuchs who introduces him to the palace cook, Bazzu and her young assistant Prea. While still ambivalent about having Helena in his house, Thomas finds he has also somehow agreed to have her younger sister, Lubna, there too. There is heartache in Thomas's past and in this story he is surrounded by attractive women but torn between lust and something more. Who can he trust? This novel is not only a great detective story but also a fabulous smorgasbord of sights, sounds, smells and tastes of fifteenth century life.

 Goodness, I haven't even mentioned the mystery. It was fabulous! There was so much going on in MOTHER'S DAY, MUFFINS, AND MURDER. From the discovery of the body, to the disappearance of said body, to re-discovery of the body, I was breathless before I was an eighth of the way through the book. And all of that was just the beginning of the rollercoaster ride this story turned out to be! 
 It's very clear how Sara Rosett has made it to ten books in this series. If she keeps writing like this, book 20 is a guarantee!

This is one of my favourite young adult novels, one that I love returning to every few years. It is a lovely story, written in a lovely voice. The two main characters, Ginny and Smitty/Michael, are very different people--yet their friendship grows in a way I find very organic and unforced. I'm not sure how this one flew under the radar when it was published in the 1990s. It's a really moving, well-written piece about the intricacy and beauty of human communication. I love it. 
 The bad? One of the criticisms I've seen leveled against it is that, at the crux of the story, there is a very unrealistic reaction to abuse. I think that's fair to say, even if it didn't bother me much when I was reading at the age for which it is intended. Also, I own a newer edition which has some unnecessarily edited passages toward the end, making the whole last quarter of the book weaker. 
 BUT I LOVE IT ANYWAY. 
 (Review from March 2012 re-read.)

Seperti judulnya, isi buku ini sebagian besar depresif, condong pada nothingness, sedikit maso, dan kesadaran akan betapa palsunya dunia ini. Duh, kok berat, ya. 
 Untuk fisik bukunya sendiri agak disayangkan, ya. Soalnya putih dan hardcover, bikin cepat kotor. Untungnya lembar yang berwarna hitam total tidak berbekas di tangan. Setidaknya pantas kalau kertasnya berkualitas, karena saya suka ilustrasi dengan latar hitam yang dibuat negatif (dan ini cukup banyak). Kan, sayang jika tintanya mudah luntur. 
 Lanjut ke isi buku. Sebetulnya tidak semua beraura muram, ada beberapa yang membuat saya berkata, 'FINALLY, POSITIVISM!' seperti favorit saya di halaman 63, tentang tubuh yang hanya sebagai wadah jiwa, maka tak ada gunanya untuk terobsesi pada tubuh (positif, kan?). Tapi memang tidak jauh-jauh dari relationship, sih. Meski ditulis dalam Bahasa Inggris, tetap saja berasa lokal, karena ada beberapa diksi yang terasa seperti 'menginggriskan Bahasa Indonesia'. Teh Botol dan Lontong Cap Gomeh juga dapat tempat di sini. Yang terasa Indonesianya antara lain frasa 'when you eat a McDonald's burger but forget to take the pickle.' karena setahu saya pickle itu khasnya burger sana, dan kurang lebih seperti sambal untuk orang kita--menjadi makanan yang dikangenin saat bepergian. Americans love their pickles. 
 Kalau kamu suka karya yang gelap dan ilustrasi gaya pop mural, mungkin saja buku ini adalah jodoh kamu.

Buck is just a regular dog who enjoys the company of his master the Judge and his other dogs. When Buck is unfortunately dognapped by the Judge's gardener and sold to a man in a red sweater, Buck's life is turned upside down. He is forced to become a sled dog and must learn to survive in the wilderness of the Alaskan klondike. Will Buck survive? Read on and find out. 
 This was a pretty good/sad read and my first ever read by author Jack London. I enjoyed this tale about an animal trying to survive and find freedom from its human captors. This book will tear at your heart-strings and make you want to read more. I also enjoyed the illustrations in this edition too. If you like animal stories and classic books, definitely give The Call of the Wild a check out for yourself. This book can be found at your local library and wherever books are sold.

To my delight, American Vampire starts out as far from "paranormal romance" as you can get. I - and apparently netGalley - would classify it as horror, in which the everyman main character just happens to be a vampire. That's kind of awesome. I mean, it's nice to read a book involving vampires where the plot doesn't hang on some character discovering another character they care for is one, or discovering they themselves are unexpectedly supernatural and have a key role to play in some future conflict. Nope, here, the protagonist Graf knows very damn well he's a vampire, and while there is a period of ignorance for the secondary characters to that fact, when it is revealed, it's not a plot-stopping event. Er, well it is kind of plot-relevant, but in a more unusual way. 
 But I'm getting ahead of myself. The protagonist here - I hesitate to say hero because for the vast majority of the book he's a very reluctant one - is Graf, the quintessential city pretty-boy who also happens to drink blood. On the vampire scale, he's somewhere around Spike circa Season Four: not a mad, bloodthirsty psychopath, but not a whimpering, angsty vampire with a soul, either. He's a dick, he doesn't care much for humans, and he'll kill them if he has to, but mostly he just wants to party. 
 Awesome. I have to admit, I really enjoyed Grif (er, I read him as Grif the first time and just stuck with it. The association was too much fun to ignore) as a character. He's an unabashed lying bastard who will con and kill you if it benefits him, and would probably be the charming bad guy in any other series, but here he makes for a good anti-hero. What's cool about American Vampire is that we get to see behind the charming facade - thankfully not (well, initially) to the marshmallow underneath, but to the panicky, amusingly self-serving asshole a bit out of his depth. 
 American Vampire does well putting Grif out of his element, in this situation he can neither understand nor control, with these people he doesn't get along with but is obligated to by circumstance, in a county with a monster bigger and badder than he is. Grif isn't accustomed to situations like this, and all he wants to do once he enters the small, appropriately-named town of Penance, Ohio, is get himself out by any means necessary. It may sound kind of weird to say, but it's nice seeing a vampire grapple with conflict not for some altruistic motive or lover, but for himself... 
 Read more at You're Killing.Us.

Cherishing Destiny is about a post apocolyptic time when not just humans but supernatural beings romed the earth, coping with the loss of many and dealing with the trials and tribulations of the ever alterning climate as a result of massive solar flares. 
 The book started out with a girl in a cave hurt. Not much else is said about this girl and very few chapters mention her in her own pov. The rest of the book mainly focused on the day in a life of two vampires and a human girl who was their companion. The begning was very slow to draw my interest. The way the first few chapters was written made it hard for me to read at first. But after a while I settled in and actually found myself enjoying some of the story. Here's why I gave it three stars. 
 The writing wasn't consistent, I had a lot of questions later because it seemed like after the half way point random facts were being added to help build the story but it was very sudden in the way that the information was introduced not like a build up for a series. I think the scenes needed to be built up more. There was a lot of jumping around and random droplets of internal dialouge which just didnt fit. Also another thing that pulled me from the story was the language. Sometimes I read dialogue that didn't match with the character. A two year old can barely speak let alone say full sentences like It's okay. 
 There was also a lot of repetitive wording that pulled me from the story. The author would explain something then explain it again. I get that this is a first book in a series and that it is a first novel. So that said its not a bad first novel.

First up: Hellboy, Batman & Starman beat up a bunch of Nazis who are trying to bring Lovecraftian horrors into our world. Hijinks & good times aplenty! For example: 
 Starman (upon viewing impending elder god): Whoa, he's a big boy. 
 Nazi: And many-sided. 
 Starman: Now that was from Lovecraft. Don't be trying to impress me with watered-down H.P. 
 On the other hand, The Ghost/Hellboy story is kinda dumb. The old Marvel Team-Up formula (heroes meet, fight due to stupid misunderstanding, eventually figure out that they're stupid, join forces & go defeat bad guy(s)) should be left for old issues of Marvel Team-Up. Mignola is a better storyteller than that.
Brilliant pretty much sums it up.

I re-read slash listened through this in free audiobook format from audiolivre.fr. It was all rather adorable, although reading again as an adult i cringed and cringed at the classism. The book is not in favour of maltreatment of the poor, per se, but it *is* vastly in favour of the rich staying rich or getting richer - Sarah deserves a life of luxury because that's what she was born to. 
 I found myself wishing for an alternate story where the diamond mine never paid out, but Uncle Tom searched out his friends' daughter anyway, because of a sense of justice, and he and Sarah have to adopt a lower-middle class lifestyle - and Sarah's experience as a pauper has taught her to value small comforts so she is able to comfort Uncle Tom and change his perspective or something equally moral but less... gross.
Very intense, and often creepy. Definitely a good thriller! I realized what the twist would be fairly early, but unsuspecting readers will be surprised.

The fun in this wordless picturebook is just answering the question: What are these pigs up to now? Once I realized what they were up to, then it was: How will they do it? Panoramic illustrations and a fairly distant zoom on the scenes makes each spread a rich experience with details to savor, and when paired with a short and wide trim size (10x6 inches) each spread feels larger. 
 I'm glad Enchanted Lion is willing to take a risk with interesting formats and ideas!

Frontier Highlander Vow of Love is the fourth book in Ms.Wiley's epic American Wilderness Series Romances. It continues the gripping saga of the courageous men and women who faced the constant dangers and hardships of traveling to and settling in Kentucky in 1797. 
 As with any series, readers anticipate an enjoyable read with each new book. Sometimes books fall short of readers' expectations for one reason or another. This is certainly not the case with Frontier Highlander Vow of Love. 
 Ms. Wiley fulfills readers' expectations with heart wrenching moments of danger, thrilling scenes of fast-paced action, and character portrayals which run the gamut of loving and honorable to abhorrent and murderous. 
 Wiley's writing style is comparative to classic novels which have stood the test of time. Readers are caught up in her memorable tales of life, death, honor, love, and hate. Her writing is gripping and holds the reader spellbound until the end. They are books to be savored and read again. 
 Like Manu Forti, meaning "with a strong hand", the clan motto of the Mackay clan in Frontier Highlander Vow of Love, Ms. Wiley's writing skills are powerful and compelling and her books are not to be missed. 
 I received a copy of Frontier Highlander Vow of Love from the author for an honest review.

Originally posted at novelcravings.wordpress.com 
 Six of Crows by Leigh Bardugo 
 Source: Purchased copy from Amazon 
 Link to the author: http://www.leighbardugo.com/index1.html 
 Rating: 5 out of 5 stars 
 Buzz Words: Heist, Theif, Wraith, Magic, Revenge 
 My thoughts: 
 Where do I even begin? I'm just going to say in advance, that this is not going to be an intellectual review but more like all the reasons you MUST READ this book. I was excited to read Six of Crows because I already loved Leigh Bardugo's other books but the hype had me worried, but let me tell you, this book exceeded the hype. This book made me laugh, a lot, it made me cry, my heart raced, and I often caught myself holding my breath - It was a hell of a ride! 
 When you want to free a scientist, one who has created a drug that could plunge the world into chaos, out of a maximum security prison, who do you call? Kaz Brekker, a brilliant schemer and the slums top player. Inej, once an acrobat and now a swift death you never see coming. Mattias, a patriotic and pissed off witch hunter. Nina, a sassy heartrenderer looking for forgiveness. Jesper, a man with quick wit and a quicker trigger finger. And Wylan, a runaway full of surprises. Together they try to pull off the heist of a lifetime. 
 I feel like Bardugo must have been a gangster in a previous life because she wrote about the gang and the slums so so well. The characters, the behaviors, the atmosphere it was all amazing and consistent. When an author writes like that everything on the page just comes alive, for me it was like being right there in Ketterdam. And I loved Ketterdam, I loved everything about this expansion on the grishaverse. The story is told in a multiple point of view format and that isn't always a good thing in my experience but again Barudgo did it perfectly. I thought six characters was a lot, that only one or two would be complex and leave an impression on me. Boy was I wrong. Without any one of them this would not have been the same story. This band of misfits were so endearing to me, I loved them all. They all had so much baggage, and rich back stories. I often found myself reading a line and thinking "Yup, that's something (Mattias) would do" Bardugo knew her characters so well that every action rang true to their nature. Her writing just blew me away and each chapter she did it over again! And the banter between the characters constantly had me laughing, the wit and sarcasm was right up my alley. Needless to say for me, this was a very character driven story, but the other dynamics of this book weren't weak by any means. It was action packed, captivating and intense. From page one I was hooked, and the story never let me go! The plot wasn't too fast or too slow for my taste and I loved the twists at every other turn of the page. I can't stand a predictable book. Can we talk about the romance for a minute? Okay, yes it was a little unrealistic that all the characters would pair up but who cares? I loved all the relationships in Six of Crows. The chemistry between Mattias and Nina especially. Their story was just so beautiful and heartbreaking it was like a Romeo and Juliet but with a second chance. A part of me is scared to read the second book because I know one of the couples must end up unhappy and I want them all to be together! Speaking of the second book -I certainly didn't see that ending coming. Of course I knew there had to be something big at the end to leave me fiending for the next book but I didn't predict that particular outcome. However, I have no complaints except that I NEED CROOKED KINGDOMS. This book was everything I hoped for and so much more. 
 If you are still doubting how good this book is, know that I rarely ever re-read a book and I would re-read this again right now. I will re-read it before Crooked Kingdoms and I think I will be re-reading it for years to come. 
 What I liked: 
 Everything! Mostly the characters and their chemistry, it was incredible. They had flaws, quirks, baggage and scars. I will never forget these characters, I feel like I know them and have hung out with them. And the banter between them was just flawlessly human. 
 What I disliked: 
 Um... that Crooked Kingdoms isn't in my hands now? That it is only a duology? That I can't go back and read Six of Crows for the first time again? 
 Would Recommend To: 
 This book is like Oceans Eleven meets Gangs of Newyork meets Mistborn. So If you enjoyed any of those, Bardugo's Grisha series or books about heists this book is for you. 
 Favourite Quote: 
 SO MANY! 
 "Better terrible truths, than kind lies" - Inej 
 "I wouldn't trust you to tie my shoes without stealing the laces, Kaz." - Nina 
 "He needed to tell her...what? That she was lovely and brave and better than anything he deserved. That he was twisted, crooked, wrong, but not so broken that he couldn't pull himself together into some semblance of a man for her. That without meaning to, he'd begun to lean on her, to look for her, to need her near. He needed to thank her for his new hat." - Kaz

What I thought: Of Poseidon was one of my favourites from last year, so I had really high expectations for Of Triton, but Anna Banks didn't fail. This one is super exciting because so much happens in so little time. Anna Banks packs everything into this 240 page book - romance, loss, betrayal and many more surprises! Grom and Nalia are reunited. But Nalia returning to the Syrena certainly causes a rift between the houses. Rayna and Emma are stuck on land, while everyone sorts things out. But of course, our heroine has to save the day, using her Gift of Poseidon. All our favourite characters are back, and each more lovable than last time! The one thing that annoyed me in this book though, was Emma. For most of the book, she acts like a bratty child and even she knows it. There are also some more exciting developments in the story, and we also learn more about Nalia. 
 But my absolute favourite part of this whole book was King Antonis. He brought the humor and he became my favourite character and my favourite parts of the book. 
 If you liked Of Poseidon then you are going to love Of Triton too! 
 The Good: Of Triton was just as amazing as the first book, which made reading this super easy! 
 The Bad: Having to wait another year for the next book!! 
 Rating: 5 bookstacks
It was May, historically her month of choice for upending my universe.

I did not expect to get emotional over this book. I didn't expect to fly through it in a day. But there I sat, in a cafe, trying very hard not to just start crying whenever Mia watched her loved ones interact with her. 
 I think this book did a good job dealing with music; to be honest, I've found that most authors don't deal with music too well. It feels name-droppy (see also Nick & Norah's Infinite Playlist) or just... ill-fitting. But Forman writes about music in a way that I found unpretentious and believable. I also enjoyed how Mia was not Not Like Other Girls, even though she clearly isn't quite like her peers. She doesn't have the special snowflake-y ness that accompanies that, which I really appreciated. 
 I also thought the relationship--I hesitate to say just "romance"--between Adam and Mia played out. This isn't just a story of their love. We see them fight, too. They go through tough times, and yet they still come out okay. I think there are too many books that are like "blah blah suddenly RELATIONSHIP PERFECT," and to be honest I can't think of many books where the protagonist stays with one partner all the way through the book. (Generally speaking, they end up with someone at the end, or they break up with their current partner towards the beginning. I don't know. I thought this was a nice way to buck that trend.) Even though Adam lets Mia go and lets her know that it's okay to leave, which I guess could be seen as a breakup, it's not made clear at the end of the book. 
 I'm not entirely sure how I feel about the ending, though. I don't mind Adam and Mia being in love. I really don't. Not too many people find true love when they are teenagers, but fine, maybe they do. I didn't quite know about it really only being Adam's love that saves Mia, though. I wanted Mia to wake up for Adam and Kim and the rest of her family. Alternatively, I wanted Teddy to survive, so Mia feels like she can come back for him and be his family, even after she has already lost so much. I don't know. I loved Kim's comment that Mia still has a family even after everyone else has died, but she doesn't make that decision until Adam comes and talks to her. Before that, she's absolutely ready to leave, and the about face felt a little strange. I had a feeling that Mia was going to make the choice to live all throughout the book--not necessarily just based on the fact that there was a sequel, but there's a fight in Mia that I found engaging. She wasn't just going to let it slip out of her hands. But so much of this book is about Mia's relationship with her biological family, and I wanted to see the fight come back for her because of them in combination with Adam and Kim, etc. Mia's parents and her brother are so heavily involved in her story that it's easy to see why she doesn't want to live without them, but I thought that maybe she could learn to survive without them, or decide to live as a way to honour their memory or their sacrifice, if that makes sense, not just for her boyfriend. I think that aspect of the ending really irritated me, which is why I knocked off at least one star. 
 This book was a breeze to get through, but it's also terribly short. When I reached the ending, I assumed there was more; instead, I got there and thought, "That's it? That's it?" Yeah, okay, Mia goes through a lot, but the ending felt quite abrupt. (You can also see more of my ending gripes under that giant spoiler thing.) I don't know, the structure of the book was super engaging and I liked all the flashbacks vs. present stuff, but... ehhhhhh. 
 I don't regret reading this book. I just wish it had been a bit better, though. I would give it 3.5 stars, but I don't want to round this up to four. Still, I am intrigued enough to want to read the sequel.
