I'll be reviewing on each novella separately. 
 The first novella, One Little Prayer, included one of the most adorable little girls I have ever read about. Her mom's story was nice, but there was a bit of a rushed feel to it, especially with James and his spiritual turn-around. I guess that is to be expected in a novella though. One more thing... this one didn't fit into the "farmer" theme that I was expecting. Maybe more of a simple post-Civil War historical. 3 stars 
 The Tie That Binds is a great little story about God bringing a family together unexpectedly and in His own special way. I like Orphan Train stories but, again, this wasn't a "farmer" themed novella per se. The abrupt change in Frank's spiritual life is understandable, given the circumstances and his previous thoughts about what he needed, and Emma's reliance on prayer was believable. I really liked this one. 4.75 stars, only falling short of 5 because how can you write a story about a seamstress and not even mention the wedding dress??? ; ) 
 A Homesteader, a Bride, and a Baby finally included a farmer's story. The situation was sad, but I still thought the main characters were giving and loving and real. I don't like a contrived reason to get married, but I understand that it happened this way back in the late 1800s. 4 stars 
 The Applesauce War was a nice little story based on a silly scheme by two dads that got out of control. I liked the legal questions (wish there was even more detail on this) and people coming together to pray for their families. I particularly liked the main characters in this one but again, not a farmer's bride. 3.5 stars 
 Sunshine Harvest made me think about citrus farming in a new light. However, I found the romance rushed and somewhat unbelievable. Although I can understand that significant loss sometimes makes people rush toward someone else to ease the pain, it seemed unlikely that this woman -- with her animosity toward Christians -- would fall for a preacher AND renew her faith in a matter of days. This one could have been a full length novel to more fully and realistically explore the character development. The mother character was also disappointing and annoyingly incapable -- I can't imagine not being part of decisions that affect my life or being as fragile as she, so it is difficult to empathize with the mother widow beyond the loss of her husband. And, I hate to harp on it, but this story was about a farmer's DAUGHTER who then became the farmer/owner herself. I can understand the publisher wanting variety, but the title of this collection is misleading and mostly inaccurate. 1.5 stars (low because of the preaching and lack of realism, but higher than one star because of the glimpse into citrus farming) 
 New Beginnings was an intriguing story that had me pulling for both of the main characters. Again, we see the power of praying with others, and sticking with your commitments regardless of what the new day brings. And, we finally have a farmer's bride as the focus of the novella. 4 stars 
 Overall, this collection was worth reading, as long as you are aware and don't mind that the title is misleading.

Every time Katy Regnery releases a new book I get a serious case of the grabby hands. And it's no wonder with her churning out amazing romance like a damn pez dispenser. When it was time to say goodbye to her beloved English brothers, I felt like a piece of my soul was dying. I had gotten so attached to those characters and their amazing love stories that I couldn't fathom not being in that world anymore. Then Katy was like "SURPRISE B*TCH! HERE'S SOME NEW BROTHERS FOR YOU!" Like they say, when God closes one door, he opens a window and then promptly lets in those sexy bastard Winslow brothers and all is right in my stupid life! 
 As with a few of the English brothers and their gals, Bidding features a couple who have known each other previously. Brooks and Skye have been acquaintances since they were teens. Through the years their acquaintance evolved into a semi-friendship as Skye became his mechanic working at the marina her father owns. They have a little bit in common built in but it mainly stops at boating stuff. When Brooks approaches Skye about making a winning bid at a charity auction where a date with the man himself is up for grabs, he stops at nothing to make sure she's the only one he'll be spending a week long excursion with...except there is no romantic intentions on his part at all which sucks for Skye because she's had it bad for him since she was a girl. *Le sigh* That's how it always works. She wants him but he can't see past her baggy overalls and grease stained fingers. 
 Hmm... Brooks. I think I'll start off talking about him because he was sort of a mixed bag of "wtf" and a little bit of "Aww's" that had me confused at times to how I really felt. He's the eldest of the Winslow clan and when their beloved patriarch died suddenly of a supposed heart attack when he was just 17, Brooks had to step up and help care for his younger siblings. Very noble and selfless of him but surprisingly he made quite a name for himself. An ex-Olympian and highly sought after bachelor who avoids ANY and ALL romantic relationships choosing instead to bang high dollar whores. *ahem* excuse me, "Escorts". This is one of those "WTF" things I spoke of a minute ago that had me scratching my head. He's rich, he's single, and the ladies are literally clawing at each other to get a piece of his man meat but he chooses to pay for it. Why? That's a question I asked myself and the not so simple answer is that because of his fathers sudden death at a young age, Brooks is terrified of following the same path so he avoids getting involved with someone because he refuses to leave behind a grieving family. Seems legit so we'll go with it. Now the prostitute/whore/escort *cough* sluts *cough* thing really bothered me for a good bit of this book. I get disgusted by guys who find it necessary to bone a different woman every day. And yeah it took a while to warm up to Brooks but seeing how utterly devastated he was to face his own supposed mortality and the gut wrenching loneliness he had to choke down daily while everyone around him was happily involved, made me thaw out a little. Brooks was a good guy, if a little clueless and short sighted especially when it came to Skye. 
 It's true what they say about love being right under your nose. It literally was for Brooks for YEARS. Skye reminds me of myself in a lot of ways. She's one of those versatile females who can get down and dirty and play rough but she also cleans up nice. When she's given free reign with Brooks' credit card to get something nice for the charity auction she's entirely clueless about fashion and accessories. Thankfully she's befriended by resident gay Clay. WHO. I. LOVED. Talk about an amazing secondary character that demands to be seen. Clay was fantastic and essentially becomes a close confidant to Skye. This sweet girl didn't have an easy life either. Raised by her father after her cheating mother left them both and headed West to pursue her "career" and left Skye with enough emotional scars to keep Dr. Phil busy. It's not made any easier with her prick of a boyfriend excluding her from their plans to sail the world together. I really liked Skye's character and with all the odds stacked against her I desperately wanted something good to happen for her. She was very smart and intuitive for a woman so young with limited experiences but it worked for me. I hated that it took her getting dressed up for Brooks to open his eyes because she was such a great woman and deserved for someone to see her regardless of what she looked like but I guess it's understandable in a lot of ways. On one hand she didn't have a female role model to help her with girly things and get her out of that tomboy stage but on the other hand she was so naturally gorgeous and charming it should have been a no-brainer... but I digress. 
 A week long boat trip with two people desperate to keep their distance for different reasons and a boatload of sexual tension makes for some exciting reading. This one was emotional and tenderly romantic and so far the Winslow brothers seem to be off to a good start. In my personal opinion I probably won't rank Brooks high up on the list when it's all said and done. I didn't really click with him like I did with most of the English brothers (minus Alex) which is bound to happen eventually. You can't win them all but the beauty of Regnery's writing is like bad pizza. Even when it's bad, it's still good. (That's a compliment by the way) There is always something to love about her stories no matter what and for me with Bidding, it was seeing the resiliency between these Winslow siblings and how they come together when times are hard and have each others backs. There is something inherently endearing about a close family and I am looking forward to seeing what's in store for the other boys. I usually close my reviews praising this author and her work, writing, characters, plots and overall knowledge of what women are looking for in a romance novel but I'm not going to do that with this one. If you haven't jumped on the Regnery Regatta (see what I did there? Boat reference! WINNING!) then my friend, (or enemy because you suck for not reading her books) you are MISSING OUT! You should have your face on a milk carton you're missing out so bad! If I were a doctor I'd prescribe you two Regnery's and call me in the morning.

 Callie is a 7th grade student who loves everything about the theatre. She lives & breathes the backstage life all while juggling friendships and crushes. When the school announces one of her favourite musicals as that year's production, she immediately goes into set designer mode, eagerly helping out in all different departments as well. Meeting new friends and dealing with weird behaviour from old ones, Callie goes through what many young people do at that age - heartaches, heartbreaks and a lot of growing up in the process. 
 This adorable middle-grade graphic novel is a fantastic read. The drawings are vivacious and cute, with a story that is familiar, yet unique at the same time. Being a theatre tech graduate myself, the plot and setting for this graphic novel immediately caught my attention. I just knew I had to read it and Telgemeier captured so many aspects of backstage life so well - from the calling of cues over headsets to the highs and woes that can befall a live production from night to night. While I was a little disappointed at the outcome of Callie's crushing, I also commend her for establishing the route that it did as well. 
 The love that Telgemeier has for the theatre shines through in this graphic novel, and her appreciation for this craft is evident in her choice of words, her drawings and the story.

This YA story is written from the heart and draws the reader into the world of the young heroes right from the start. I love books that are written from the character's POV and this one alternates chapter by chapter between the two main characters as they tell the story. The effect is that you can't help feeling you are right there with them witnessing all the events as they unfold and feeling their emotions for yourself. 
 Young Joshua has suffered extreme bullying at school in silence for years. He had found a way to 'survive' that involved keeping to himself, avoiding his abusers as far as he could and sharing nothing of his pain with anyone. This had become a way of life for him and he expected nothing less. Then he met Eve who has fallen victim to manipulation and bullying in another way. Slowly Eve warms to Joshua, the outcast. She not only realises, with horror, what has been happening to him, but sees him for who he really is - a warm, sensitive, brave and amazing person. The two become close friends and their shared strength and understanding of each other and life enables them both to become themselves and grow emotionally - in a remarkably mature way. 
 This book would be an asset to young teenagers' classrooms or school libraries and would be a great teaching aid for those wanting to raise awareness in of the potential damage done by bullying when it is left unchecked. More than that, it demonstrates in a positive and courageous way how those who are excluded or bullied by their peers can find strength within themselves and begin to realise that they are valuable individuals who are as entitled to respect and friendship as anyone else. Sadly, many young people who suffer bullying in real life, as Joshua had in the story, have their self-esteem so eroded they find it almost impossible to turn things around. This book works as an inspiration and encouragement to them too.

 HER LADYSHIP'S CURSE was a quick, short and easy read. Lynn Viehl did a good job in constructing her version of Steampunk America in so few words, doing it in a very vivid and realistic way without sacrificing the plot and conflict of the story. Charmian "Kit" Kittredge was very succinct in giving us a short version of her backstory, connections and friendships it was quite easy to get lost in the fantasy. I haven't read Steampunk America like this, those that I've come across have a western feel to it and I'm not into that setting. Disenchanted & Co. feels very Victorian despite being set in the Indies plus there's a really good balance of magic, action and "reality" here which made the story believable to an extent. 
 The ending! OMG! Thank God I have part 2, His Lordship Possessed, otherwise I'll be thumping myself on the head in suspense and frustration due to that cliffhanger! Like WTH! After all that tension, Kit and Lucien finally had their moment and lo and behold, Lucien did a total jerk move to "protect" Kit and the afterglow hasn't even faded yet! And that's how HER LADYSHIP'S CURSE concluded. Major issues still unresolved and we readers are left feeling anger and disbelief over Dredmore's audacity and duplicity. Bah! So let me binge and I'll come back to you with my thoughts on His Lordship Possessed, hopefully LViehl will show a little bit of mercy and will leave us something nice to tide us over til His Clockwork Wolf 's release.

I'm torn between giving this book two stars or three. While the overall message was something I agree with, it certainly took a long time getting there. 
 The basic storyline is that four plane crashes occur on the same day, scattered around the globe, and three children miraculously survive. Their survival becomes fodder for religious wingnuts and conspiracy theorists around the world. 
 Things I liked: 
 The epistolary format - Written in the form of interviews, emails, news articles, letters, etc. I've always like this style, but I this time the content was a little slow moving the story along. 
 The message - I can't say what anyone else got out of it, but what I got out of it basically agrees with some of my strongest beliefs. The masses are easily led by the media, with fear being the strongest emotion that draws people together. There's more, of course, but I don't want to give too much away. 
 Things I didn't like: 
 The pacing - It dragged. I kept reading because I thought, mistakenly, that surely something dramatic would eventually happen. I can imagine that this started out as a top-notch short story or novella that was expanded into a novel. At 476 pages, it's a pretty long horror novel where nothing singularly horrible happens. The horror is in the possibilities and eventualities. 
 The missed opportunity - This novel could have been a lot more. It could have been truly horrible, but the way I imagine that would preclude the epistolary format, probably. I imagine it with a bit of backstory, more action in the present, and moving further into the future. That's a story I would love to read. 
 I did finish it, but I wish I had spent those 476 pages on something else.

athryn Lasky is een bijzonder succesvolle auteur, met vele boeken (meer dan honderd) en reeksen op haar naam. Onlangs voltooide ze het 16e deel in de serie De legende van de wachters. De eerste twee delen zijn inmiddels ook in Nederland uitgekomen. De ontvoering is het eerste deel, dat alles in gang zet. 
 Een jonge uil in een broedplaats van kwaad 
 In het Bosrijk van de kerkuilen woont de jonge uil Soren met zijn ouders, zijn knorrige oudere broer Kludd en de blindslang Mevrouw Plithiver, hun nesthulp. Wanneer zijn nieuwe zusje Eglantine uit het ei kruipt is iedereen dolgelukkig, behalve de altijd chagrijnige Kludd. Maar in het bos verdwijnen de laatste tijd steeds uilskuikens en zelfs eieren verdwijnen op mysterieuze wijze uit hun nest. 
 Hoewel Soren zich zorgen maakt om zijn kleine zusje, is juist hij degene die dat lot ondergaat. Door een vreemd ongeluk valt hij uit het nest en belandt op de grond, weerloos voor alle roofdieren die daar leven. Hij wordt echter gevonden door twee mysterieuze uilen die hem ver weg naar het St. Aegolius Internaat voor Verweesde Uilen brengen. Maar niemand is daar geinteresseerd in het feit dat hij helemaal geen wees is en dat blijkt voor meer uilen te gelden. Het internaat is een vreemde plek vol regels en strenge straffen voor wie ze overtreedt en de 'school' lijkt meer op een strafkamp. Behalve het ontvoeren van uilskuikens, het uitbroeden van gestolen eieren en het hersenspoelen van hun leerlingen, houden de uilen van St. Aegolius zich ook bezig met het zoeken naar de mysterieuze spikkels, zilverkleurige korrels die voor hen van onschatbare waarde zijn.

A few authors over the course of the past few years have recently stood out above the normal, literary crowd--for me, anyways. And the thing I noticed about these authors is that they all seem to write darker fiction. If I had to say, a good representation of these authors is: Roberto Bolano, Cormac McCarthy, Castle Freeman, Jr., and now, Daniel Woodrell. 
 These authors make up a class of writers that I have termed Brutal Poets. Their use of language invokes a visceral response from the reader, sounds sometimes biblical or archaic, but never forced. The way they describe a landscape that mimics the inner feelings of characters is alarming and disorientating because of its precision and perfection. Basically, these authors seem to really know what it is that they are writing about. 
 Woodrell, a previous unknown to me before I saw the adaptation of his novel on DVD, is a master storyteller. Terse and sparse, his novel WINTER'S BONE is a punishing reward of a read. The story takes place over a few days in the Ozarks, Appalachia country. Ree Dolly needs to find Jessup, her daddy. He's skipped out on court, and has put his house and acreage up for collateral for his bond. The problem is something isn't right. He's gone missing. And Ree begins to understand more about where she lives exactly, and who the people really are that populate her family and community. Characters like Thump and Uncle Teardrop and even Ree's Mom add a depth to this story that brings it past a "missing-person" story or a "murder mystery." 
 From the moment Ree takes it upon herself to find out the truth about her father, to the moment she has the emotional revelation at the end of the story with Uncle Teardrop, this bleak novel will keep you mesmerized, wanting to turn pages as fast as you can until you have reached the staggering and horrifying conclusion. 
 Don't do this. Don't ruin such a great experience by consuming it whole. Nibble at the book. Let your mind digest it. Savor it. Like a death row inmate being given their last meal, taste every juicy word on every page. Drink up every image and scene. There are plenty of other books out there to scarf down as fast as you can. Not this one. 
 Warning: be prepared. Oftentimes there are bleak moments like when Ree is beaten by the Milton sisters, and presented in a barn to Thump. When Ree comes to, she and a girl named Megan exchange these words: 
 Megan squatted, patted Ree's face, and said, "Whatever are we to do about you, baby girl? Huh?" 
 "Kill me, I guess." 
 "That idea has been said already. Got'ny other ones?" 
 "Help me. Ain't nobody said that idea yet, have they?" 
 This scene still makes my flesh get goose bumps. 
 (VERY HIGHEST RECOMMENDATION)

Wow, okay i had a reading marathon i think and read Dark Swords series then went straight into Dark Warrior series.. how happy was I when i read series is to be continued this summer! 
 For those who dont know Dark Swords is set in the 17th century and the story of Warriors (Higlanders with a god inside them) fighting against the Evil Druid Dredrie(?sp) 
 Each Book is a romance/paranormal story for want of a better word, but the book do follow on from each other and i loved how we never lost sight of the early characters who we fell in love with. 
 Dark Warriors I think is a love or hate sequel..personally Im firmly on the love side lol. In the final book of Dark Sword Dredrie is catapulated into the future by an another evil Druid. Unfortuantley Ian one of the warriors is pulled along with her (wont say why as would ruin the story lol) 
 Each of the warriors has a special ability, one of the Broc, can find anyone anywhere, anytime and he finds the year (2012) the Dredrie is now in. So 4 of the mighty warriors have a spell cast on them to arrive in this modern world. 
 Parts of it made me giggle and how quick they picked things up, and adept they became so quickly! But the books are fantasy so, so what! It didnt spoil it for me, in fact it made it nice to see the humour in some of the warriors. 
 Hence they all end uo making their way to McLeod Castle , where their comrades have waited 400 years for them (The Warriors are immortal, the Druids have cast a spell so their wives are as well) 
 The rest fo the series (so far ) has been them battling against the evil Dreidrie, the nasty Evil Druid Declan and off course finding love and sex along the way. 
 I know some dont like how it has come to the present day but it hasnt bothered me as a lot of the 'old ways' are still there. 
 I LOVE how we still have the Lucan, Quinn and Fallon and their wives in the storyline. So looking forward to the summer to carry on this great series. 
 BTW For those who know me, will tell you i would never normally read any of these books about Magic etc.. i must be one of the few who hasnt read Twilight lol. 
 What grabbed me was the books were about Highlanders, and who cant resist a man in a kilt and also Donna Grant was recommended to me. No doubt about it will tell my friends to read but i would say start at the beginning.. each book can be read as a standalone but so much better when reading the whole series.

 and

Rob and Gamlyn are part of me and I need them to be together!

The first half of the book is set in the Wode which i loved as stated before the book sparkles when Robyn and Gamelyn are together. The second half of the book is flash reading as you desperately wait for them to find each other again as bad stuff always happens when their apart.

 Re-Read 28/08/2016 
 So I see all the Marion and Gamelyn moments now and I think I understand a lot more of the deeper layers in Winterwode now that I have read the book three times. The puzzle pieces are coming together and I cannot wait to see where Summerwode leads us with the Summerlord taking his place in his Wode. I took my time over the book really saving the beautiful writing style that Hennig has and appreciating how each strand of the story comes together to create a not yet complete tapestry.

"Lust, gluttony, greed, sloth, wrath, envy and pride. The Cynfell brothers are the very embodiment of a sinful existence. But could the right woman change that?" 
 #3 in the wildly popular, "Cynfell Brothers" series. Each story can be read as a stand alone. Although, I would suggest reading "Sinful Confessions" and "Sinful Deeds" as well. I read this story in yes, one setting. 
 Greed, is young Lord Pierce Cynfell's sin, greed and gambling until he meets Evelyn Chesworth, then all bets are off.... 
 I liked how the author put an older Duchess with a younger Lord. Oh, and sparks doth fly, but there is danger lurking. When Evelyn proposes a three month proposition to Pierce in order to pay off his gambling debts, he can't resist the offer...to become her lover for three months. 
 Fast paced, quick read filled with hot, steamy passion, danger, a big secret, blackmail, and what the power of love can accomplish in another wayward Cynfell. Greed may have started a bargain but can love end a lifetime of loneliness and greed? 
 Fans of Samantha Holt's tales of love, passion, and secrets are sure to enjoy seeing another Cynfell brought to his knees and lose his desire for greed or lose everything in the process. Another enjoyable, enchanting and satisfying read. Can't wait to see which Cynfell brother is next in this fantastic and unique series. Ms. Holt is a very impressive storyteller, who creates unique, intriguing and entertaining stories, filled with passion, love and romance. A must read for any and all fans of unique Historical romance with charming and passionate characters and intriguing and gratifying stories. Well done! Another hit for Ms. Holt!

In 82' I was preoccupied with the task of being young as well as finishing my education in the merchant navy. 
 In those days - when at sea - the daily news were compiled and 'edited' by the radio officer and distributed on a single sheet of A4 paper pinned to the bulletin board in the mess. And to be honest, you would not find me in front of that reading it. 
 (To the youngsters: Once upon a time the internet did not exist. Amazingly we survived to tell the tale ;-) 
 So the 'big picture' of the state of the world was not all that clear to me. 
 To to read about the course of events in this - in many respects - strange war has been very interesting. And put more than a few things in perspective. 
 For me this book was a very good read

While Crave Me is book 2 in the Luminous series, it can absolutely be read as a standalone. With that being said, I enjoyed the first book so I was exited to see where Stacey Lynn would take us with Simon and Chloe. 
 What I liked about this story was that they had a past and it's almost like double taboo to some. BDSM and a sister's ex. That might just get some heads turned. Chloe has been infatuated with Simon since the moment she and her sister laid eyes on him. Unfortunately for her, he picked her sister. Even years after their relationship ended, Chloe she had feelings for him. So when she went to him asking him to train her as a submissive, you knew there were going to be some attachments from the start. 
 I won't rehash the book. I think it takes away from some of the reader's experiences and puts some unfair expectations before the first word is read. What I will tell you is that this book is HOT. Just like with the first book, the sexy times are smoking hot and will have you clenching your thighs. It's highly recommended that you read this at home unless you enjoy discomfort in public. You know what I'm talking about. :) 
 I like that Simon isn't your typical Dom that most write about. Sure, he is when it comes to playing the role but there isn't some dark story behind his desires and he isn't some billionaire. He's a teacher and a hockey coach and that makes him way hotter in my opinion. More realistic and quite frankly a better fantasy! So many things you can go with. 
 I've always enjoyed Stacey Lynn's writing. It flows easy and has the right descriptive balance that I look for. With Crave Me, she delivers us a smoking hot love story full of dominance, sass and whit. Pick it up, I think you might just like it.

 It's not really a review just my thoughts on this book. 
 I must admit it was a fun ride. I mean the whole series and especially because of that I expected an epic end and... I don't think I was given one. 
 I don't know i have some issues with this book and I don't feel it was the right ending. Cassandra Clare wrote over 700 pages book and I feel over two hundred of them was just forces because she wanted this book to be the hugest so far. Look at City of Glass, that was originally a last book in The Mortal Instruments series. It was 500+ pages long and it was 500+ pages pact with action and this is how the series should be finished. I expected an epic battle here as well. As far as I am concered - I hardly doubt it was that epic (was it even a battle at all). I am in love/hate relation ship with the final act. Meaning - Sebastian/Jonathan being stabbed and then magically he had changed so much he decided to regret what he has done. Like whaaaaaat a minute since when stabbing people changes them so much? I liked Jocelyn/Jonathan scene tho. She cried even tho she shouldn't - he was a monster, but she was also his mother after all. It's mother think to do - cry when the child is lost. And at least, she had a chance to say goodbye. 
 Also there is that one think I will never be over with. Cassandra Clare claimed so so many times she is going to kill some of the main characters. Can someone show me which main characters died? Because either my edition is incomplete or she killed no one. Not even Jocelyn or Luke. Unless we are counting the Endarkened or Sebastian but he was obvious to die and I don't think there were main characters among Endarkened????? 
 Also ALL the references to The Infernal Devices. Okay they weren't THAT direct which is a good thing mainly - there was never said Zachariah is Jem, but I think for a person who hasn't read The Infernal Devices and is going to read afterwards and uses their brain a bit it's gonna be obvious who is who [especially after Tessa's question about Emma and if she will learn to play violin c'mon she is Carstairs...] . 
 I am quite glad how the things ended for Simon tho okay, not everything because he didn't have to lose all the memories it was sooooooo sad, as if Clare decided to make their characters suffer maybe not that much because of war but by looking at his best friend who has no idea who they are.... His sacrifice was really really amazing and for once he was a hero. But I Magnus should've taken his place and die. Seriously Magnus dying would be such a cool way to show even immortality doesn't last forever 
 For now this review-kind-of-thing seems to be hate but it's not it's just easier to me write about what i didn't like than about what i did like i don't know. 
 But of course there are things I like. Clace relations were quite cute. I liked how they trust each other and such... 
 And personally, the most beautiful thing in the book was Tessa giving Herondale ring to Jace - not directly but still. It would be even more beautiful if she gave it to him herself. She is his grand-grand-grand-(no idea how many grand's i should put)-mother after all. 
 Also after Simon lost his memories, and named his band The Mortal Instruments, it was so cute and cool hint - look there is still hope for him. Better than brutally taking him aside and saying 'look simon you lost memories, we are your friends' idk i like it in the way it was in the book.

Darius Thorne is a professor. A scholar. He's also a very handsome man. His life was quiet and full of education until the day she arrived. Nearly frozen and scared to death, Isabel turned Darius' world around in a matter of seconds. Feeling protective of her from the start, Darius soon learned Isabel was an abused woman. Signs of a fresh flogging on her back and the nightmares she had confirmed his suspicion. In no time at all, Darius had lost his heart to "Helen". He knew he shouldn't get so close, but she was everything he'd ever wanted in a woman. Helen was terrified of being found and receiving an even more severe punishment than the one she ran from. It takes time but she does learn to trust Darius and his staff. As with all good things, there is an end. Darius and Helen will fight for their love. They both only hope they can tame the beast who enters their loving world. 
 Renee Bernard really did an excellent job of incorporating the abuse into the story without making the story only about the abuse. I was amazed at the love, kindness and caring Helen receives from the people whose lives she is suddenly dumped into. You'll fall in love with Darius because he's that quiet, bookish type you saw in college or high school and wanted to approach but were afraid you'd scare him off. The characters are terrifically designed and fit this book in such a wonderful way. I highly recommend you check out this latest book in Renee Bernard's series "The Jaded Gentlemen". This book knocked me off my feet in a fantastic way! 
 I found no issues. 
 I gave this one 5 out of 5 books because as a former abused woman, I'd love to have been in Isabel's shoes where Darius is concerned.

I wanted to love this book. I thought that I would from the premise. Unfortunately about halfway through, I realized that it was taking me about twice as long to read it as an average book of this length. I felt as if I was reading a first draft with great ideas, some great lines...and some filler that needed editing. 
 I would love to see this book revamped, with some final revising. I know I could love it more, and I think that's what frustrates me the most. I'm sure I'm being harder on the book than I usually would be, because I know it could be better. There were some beautiful lines thrown in, and the Kindle popular highlights seems to agree with me on some of the lines being entirely mesmerizing. 
 Eden is an entirely unlikeable high school senior, who is somehow relatable as well. That boggles my mind a bit, but despite having some moments where I related to her, I still didn't like her. I spent the entire novel yelling at her in my brain, just wishing she'd grow up. Despite being obsessed with Mr. Christian, she is mostly only focused on his clothes. Get over the jacket with the elbow patches. Get over it. I also found the insta-love/lust a little overwhelming. One look at Mr. Christian and Eden was changing her entire life. It didn't seem something that a strong popular girl would do. 
 I would like to have seen more growth between the two of them. While intense, I felt the relationship was a little flat, slightly forced. Even though Eden made her intentions perfectly clear to anyone in her class that paid attention to her, no one seemed to notice how she felt. I expect everyone to notice nearly everything the popular girls do...not just scurry away and never speak of it. 
 Overall, the book was good. I was simply left unsatisfied with the depth of the relationship between Eden and Mr. Christian.

When I requested this I was hoping for a full blown steampunk novel (based on the cover alone) that's full of a deep mythology regarding magic use, demi-gods and the like as the GoodReads write-up suggests but that really isn't the book that you get. I think that the write-up you get with this book doesn't reflect the book in it's true nature. What you get is more of a science fiction book with steampunk and paranormal elements. Don't get drawn in with the thoughts of high-brow magic, gods and demi-gods as what you actually will find is a more complex. 
 In this world we find there are three types of people, you have the Caecus (non-magic folk), the Validus (the magic users who live in various 'guilds') and the Half-Breeds, who are what you get when Caecus and Validus mix but not what I would class as demi-gods. They live a world very different to our own where the technology to 'fold' space has been created and allows for instantaneous travel between realms, and there are an awful lot of realms out there too, some claimed by various countries, some not and classed as Outlander realms. Along with this technology people live in a world where airships fill the skies and computers exist but they are different to what we know, it's the air travel and technology like the personal computers that give the book it's steampunk edge. 
 Out story begins with Wendy Braca, a young girl who comes home to find her mother has been murdered. With her father also dead Wendy finds herself in the Greenleaf Asylum For Troubled Girls and it's a place that is as unpleasant as it sounds, run by a man with a taste for abuse you can imagine what a horrible life the 'inmates' live. Here Wendy remains until the day something rather extraordinary happens to her and she is rescued from the abuse and taken in by a strange guild who introduce her to the world of magic, of The Validus. While settling into her new life as a magic user she finds out that she is now part of a guild of assassin who are determined to undermine other Validus guilds, more bizarrely she find out that she is something very unique.... Wendy is 'The Curse Breaker', the most powerful and ultimately special Validus in existence. 
 What is there to love about this book? 
 I found the book to be very different from what I was expecting and I must admit that initially I wasn't expecting the book to be quite as entertaining as it was. It had an interpreting write up but it was from an unknown to me publisher and from an author who I had no knowledge of. I chose the book on the write up alone, which was a mistake, so although it sounded like it had potential I wasn't expecting too much BUT it turned out to be better than I thought it would be. I felt there was a great sense of imagery throughout the book and that I had a real sense for the world and the surroundings. I hoped for more of a steampunk edge but the science fiction aspects overruled the steampunk elements. Saying that the sci-fi elements were well explained and I got a great feel for them. Yes, there were aspects of the book that did bug me a little (more on that later) but over-all it was a great read, easy to understand and it kept me thoroughly entertained. 
 Was there anything not so good? 
 Okay, I've told you how the write-up for Guild Assassin is bit misleading as it makes you think you're getting one book when you're actually getting something quite different and I can imagine how some readers who find themselves in the same boat I did would be pretty disheartened by this discovery, it may put them off altogether but I would suggest giving the book a go though. 
 One of things that did bother me about the book was the slow start, I can understand why the slow start is there as it allows the book to build up tempo and give the reader the opportunity to get to know Wendy and the other members of her guild, I like it when books do this in general but personally I found the beginning a little bit to slow and in places (usually around the mythology and some of the scientific stuff) it got a little bit confusing meaning I had to re-read things several times before it sunk in. 
 Another thing is the whole 'Curse Breaker' thing, I wanted to know more..... exactly what is it, what does it mean for Wendy, what does it mean for the world? I finished the book feeling that I might have missed something as I felt I didn't really know what being the Curse Breaker was. I'm hoping it will be brought to the forefront more in the next book as I really want to know more. 
 Was it an interesting read? 
 I found the book to be quite interesting as it was unlike anything I've read before and the amalgamation of the steampunk, sci-fi and paranormal elements worked quite well when put together. I didn't find any particular parts of the book to be 'boring' at all as it kept me engaged and interested throughout. 
 Was it enjoyable to read? 
 It was enjoyable to read and while it may not be the kind of book that blows me away with it's brilliance its definitely worth the read as it was very engaging and held me interest from start to finish despite leaving me with a few unanswered question, that I hope will be addressed in the next book. 
 Was it a well written book? 
 I thought it well written in general although I did find the characterisations lacked a certain sparkle that made them stand out in the crowd especially Wendy who didn't feel quite as rounded as I wanted her to be, I wanted her to be a significantly bigger character than she was considering all the trials she's been through in her life and due to her being the 'Curse Breaker'. She lacked that certain pizazz that she needed although she wasn't alone in this as I wanted to have more of a connection with all of the characters that I got which disappointed me a little. 
 The imagery the author used to show the world and surroundings was well done and I really did get a good feel for the world the characters lived in so I had no problems there at all, all good as far as I was concerned. 
 The pace of the book was good and jammed packed full of action, the language the author used was good and not overly verbose with the descriptive making the book an easy read by ways of being able to completely understand what the author was trying to portray. In my eyes is was a decent debut attempt and I am quite interested to see how things progress with the next title in the series. 
 Would you recommend it to others? 
 While I don't think this book would suit everyone I do think it is worth a read but please don't be fooled by the write-up for it, it fooled me into thinking it was a different type of book than it actually was, it's still a nice entertaining read and I am keen to read the next book in the r series to see what else life has in store for poor old Wendy..... bring it on!

 Holy shit. What a wonderful surprise. This is the best fairy tale retelling I've read in a long time. 
 It takes the idea of the story - a girl who sleeps for a hundred years and is woken by a kiss - and turns it into something heartrending and utterly believable. First off, as I said when I started this book, a Sleeping Beauty that deals with the consequences of the "princess" waking up a hundred years after her time had my interest immediately. It's not something I've seen explored a lot - in fact, one of my favorite Sleeping Beauty retellings doesn't have her losing that time at all! And the world building is fantastic. This is a sci-fi retelling, one where Rose spent a hundred years in a stasis tube. It's also one where what she missed included the world very nearly coming to an end - a complex disaster spanning many years and involving two different virulent diseases, food shortages, and reproduction becoming very, very difficult. There's also much much more involved in both the present and past of her planet and it just feels so realistic, in that there are advances and problems with those advances, contentious issues, changing trends, changing language, changing economic circumstances. It's very rich. 
 But the emotional heart of the story is Rose's coming to terms with what she has been through, and rediscovering her own story as we discover it, and finding where she fits now. And I was fully not expecting the things that did come to the surface. The story with her family is awful, and we understand how it shapes who she is, and I don't think the mark of it will ever leave her. But the idea of chosen family, and true love, is also big, and I adore the way Rose comes to understand both herself and her friends through her conversations with them. Also, the way this book deals with the love story is...pretty refreshing, actually. Their love for each other is life-changing, but it's not the giddy romance that changed them. It's the understanding, the guilt, the loss, the way they grew up, together and apart. And the uncertain ending was perfect, really; there's so much for Rose to deal with, but now she has time.

I'm a big fan of Shaun Hutson but his recent work with Hammer didn't do much for me. Monolith, his latest and first with indie press Caffeine Nights, is a return to the urban horror Hutson seems most comfortable with and proves all the more enjoyable for that. But it's certainly not his best work. 
 Basic premise has our two anti-heroes, journos Jess and Hadley, investigating a mysterious new apartment block development with a bad track record when it comes to... er... people getting killed. Owned by a notorious Russian businessman, our dashing duo sense exotic evil is afoot. Their investigations uncover a dark secret involving occultic mojo with a little Jewish mysticism thrown in for good measure. Cue lots of gore. 
 In some ways, Monolith is a bit of a rush job with a few questionable plot points, little in the way of character development and a few loose ends left dangling. That all said, Hutson's cinematic writing style and a pulpy use of short chapters and cliffhangers all make for something of a page-turner. 
 A must for fans of Huston who, like myself, have missed his inimitable brand of urban horror. For newcomers, earlier titles such as Stolen Angels, Lucy's Child or Unmarked Graves may prove better to kick off with.

Sentiz is doing horrible, evil things to everyone she touches in the kingdom, including Werrien, and things look pretty bleak. A guy from Kristina's past helps her escape many misadventures, but what are his motives? Kristina wants desperately to be re-united with Werrien, but is that possible with Sentiz's evil power? If they are re-united is there any way Werrien will ever be the same again? 
 Ms. Simcox paints an evil time in this fantasy land and the reader wonders if it's possible for her characters to escape their horrible situations. The question of whether or not good can overcome evil and the plights of the characters keep the reader turning pages. I recommend this book for those who enjoy reading about the battle of evil against good and fantasy.

I have such a soft spot for Tessa Dare. A huge reason I got back into historical romance (after a little hiatus that lasted years) was because I read 
 Romancing the Duke 
 by Tessa Dare. It sucked me in and reminded me why I love historical romance so much. Since then I've read a lot of her books, including all of the Spindle Cove series . . . except Beauty and the Blacksmith, a novella about Diana Highwood. But that has changed, because I finally read this adorable novella, and I loved it so much! 
 What's the Story: 
 Diana Highwood is the eldest Highwood sister, and she's also the most beautiful. However she has a health problem - severe asthma - which led to her widowed mother and two sisters moving to Spindle Cove. Her mother wants her to marry some titled gentleman, but Diana is more interested in the local blacksmith, Aaron Dawes. Aaron likes Diana too, but can they make a relationship work even with class differences? (I think you know the answer to that!) 
 What I Liked: 
 Spindle Freaking Cove! I love this small, unconventional town in Regency England. I love its residents, and all the quirkiness that comes with small town life. 
 Aaron is so swoon-worthy. It was so easy to understand why Diana fell for Aaron. He's hunky, with super awesome arm muscles from his work, but he's also kind and caring and handles responsibility so very well. 
 I've always loved Diana from previous Spindle Cove books. However it was just amazing to see her finally stand up for what she wants. She had enough of her mother pushing her to marry a titled gentleman, but she also wouldn't stand for Aaron being an idiot either. 
 The side-characters! Tessa Dare writes such fun and fully developed side-characters, but she especially excels at it in this series. 
 What I Disliked: 
 I wanted more! I know it's very common, but I did wish the story was longer than novella-length. Beauty and the Blacksmith is an exceptional novella, but it does have novella-related issues. 
 Final Thoughts: 
 Beauty and the Blacksmith by Tessa Dare is an excellent addition to the Spindle Cove series. It's filled with hunky heroes, independent heroines, quirky characters, and a small town we've all come to love.This review was originally posted on Quinn's Book Nook

Lauren Oliver is famous for her books for slightly older readers, particularly Delirium and Pandemonium. There are too many good YA series for me to keep up with these days, so I haven't read those, but I picked up 'The Spindlers' because it was a stand-alone book available for free from Amazon Vine. The back cover of my ARC compares it to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland & Through the Looking-Glass and Coraline, but there's really only one scene near the end that really reminded me of 'Coraline.' It's a fairly dark story, in some ways akin to the Greek myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, if that couple were a brother and sister and the sister had to go to the Underworld (here simply called Below) to rescue the brother. Like Alice, Liza is a sensible, level-headed girl who finds herself on an adventure with talking animals, strange creatures and homicidal queen. Like Alice, she finds herself equal to the challenge - even when confronted, like Harry Potter, with a 3-headed dog. Reading this, I had neither the sense that I was reading a wholly derivative retold Greek myth nor the sense that I was reading something wholly original - it falls somewhere in the middle. It touches on the issues of trust, friendship, honesty, the value of siblinghood and how children should treat their parents, but it's not overly didactic. I probably would have enjoyed this as a bedtime story when I was a middle-grade reader.

It's a little hard to believe that this is from the same author as Beautiful Creatures and the rest of the Caster Chronicles 'verse, and the still-unfinished Legion trilogy. It's a little something completely different for Kami Garcia, and it carries a similar "I want to keep going" addictive prose...but unfortunately, it fails to deliver characters I can care about to go along for the ride. I'm at a loss to see what possessed Garcia to write such a hackneyed story that checks off all the "edgy YA contemporary" boxes, particularly the dreaded "bad boy" trope. Unless perhaps it was to beat Maggie Stiefvater to writing an auto-racing-themed YA book and make Stiefvater gnash her teeth furiously over it? 
 Seriously, I hope this detour into the "real world" is only temporary, because I know Garcia can score well in paranormal fiction, and she still has to finish the Legion trilogy, doesn't she? For now, though, I'm DNFing this book after about 75 pages.

Not much left to say about Collins. He's brilliant, the way he baits us with this charming, and seemingly harmless, humor, and then right at the end we realize we've been shown the light of deep reflection on important things. 
 The new poems are just great. I remember distinctly as an American kid, digging a hole in the back yard for some reason, and my dad telling me that if you dug a hole deep enough, you would dig all the way through to China. Maybe you have a similar memory? Here's how Collins riffs off that childhood experience: 
 Orient 
 You are turning me 
 like someone turning a globe in her hand, 
 and yes, I have another side 
 like a China no one, 
 not even me, has ever seen. 
 So describe to me what's there, 
 say what you are looking at 
 and I will close my eyes 
 so I can see it too, 
 the oxcarts and all the lively flags. 
 I love the sound of your voice 
 like a little saxophone 
 telling me what I cold never know 
 unless I dug a hole all the way down 
 through the core of myself. 
 * 
 Collins is never a waste of your time.

The story is a mix of funny and thriller, and it has the merit to have sidetracked me. When we met Brian, he is a recent widower of Michael, the man he was divorcing from after he found out he was cheating him with his twin brother Brandon; Brandon and Michael accidentally died together in a car crash before they were able to have a proper closure with Brian. Now Brian is in the middle of two different hurt: he is missing his brother and husband but at the same time he is angry with them. In a burst of energy, he decides to drive until a place he does not yet know where and instead gets stranded in the middle of a mountain during a snowstorm risking hypothermia. 
 When hunky ranger Hawk rescues him, there is no doubt Brian is gay: if the sticker on his car were not clues enough, the black thong with a pink bow in the centre of a pretty bum is probably the killer clue. So when Hawk has to go pretty intimate with Brian to give him all the body warm he can gather (included that of his own dog Shadow), the fact that also Hawk is gay seems a bonus and not a problem. 
 Hawk is living in a very small mountain town, where basically there is a townhouse, a diner, a hotel and nothing more else. When the townsfolk happen to know a stranger is in town, and said stranger has slept with their resident park ranger, counting 2 plus 2 is pretty easy; despite Hawk worries to maintain his closet a secret, people around seem to have not problem with him being gay, probably they are more interested in the chance of having a new resident: if Hawk is good enough to draw another man in town, the fact that this man will sleep in Hawk's bed is not apparently a problem. 
 But Brian arrived in town running away from something, and the strange accident causing the death of both his husband and twin brother was too much a coincidence for me to think it was causal. While reading about Brian and Hawk's developing relationship, I was also searching for some clue that linked Brian to some strange event; and instead I was completely out of track, and Brian was not the man in danger of the situation. On the contrary, pretty Brian with his rainbow stickers and black thong with a pink bow will have the chance to play the role of the hero, a role that Hawk, with his Native American origins perfectly matching Brian's fetish with the Last of Mohicans, was expecting to fill. 
 As I said, there is a roller coast between danger and funny moments, all characters involved have their sudden turns, even the dog and Hawk's grandfather, the old tribe shaman... no one is behaving like you would expect, and in the end, this gives the story a light feeling, the reader is always expecting for the unexpected.

The Survivor is an action packed suspense novel with a touch of romance, the perfect combination. I was glued to the pages, trying to figure out who-did-it but to no avail. I had no idea who the villain(s) were until the end.

 "Tigo hurried into Crystal Point Methodist's ER while Ryan parked the car. He had to put cuffs on his temper. Frustration and concern for Kariss made a volatile brew. He should have insisted she stay at home and not meet with Amy. But she probably wouldn't have listened anyway. They were two stubborn women. He planned to give both of them another dose of reality if the shooting hadn't done the trick. 
 FBI Special Agent Santiago Harris, also known as Tigo, and his partner Ryan Steadman have their hands full with the investigation of a car bomb which killed a mother and her child. Was the bomb intended for them or for the husband? Although his partner Ryan is a Christian, Tigo has his own ideas about God, "I can't do the Jesus thing unless I feel it's real." 
 There were two cases to be solved...an unsolved cold case and a current case of the car bomb. Although I am not a great fan of romance the unsolved issues between Kariss and Tigo, intrigued me. I did wonder what would happen to them.

Soft , beautiful watercolors add to the ocean feel of these poems for youngsters. Some are two page spreads, others are images of a single ocean creature. The whale's fluke is splashing above the surface of the water with a shipwreck at the bottom, all in one spread which the reader turns the book to sense the enormity of the whale. For the waves, seven small frames provide different images of the many forms waves can take, along with lots of great descriptive words: 'murmer shush', 'roll green', 'strike the shore' (but none of the images show green). 
 A wide variety of images are given to the reader through descriptive phrases and give facts, such as in "Sand's Story" 'We used to be rocks,' Most verses do not rhyme, giving young poets reinforcement that poetry need not rhyme. 
 A number of unusual creatures are incuded: oarfish, and nudibranch, giving this a refreshing presentation in the sea of ocean books. The author's familiarity with the ocean is evident in her choice of descriptive phrases and words. 
 Begins with a boat launch as if we are setting off to explore the ocean, and the last poem shows a sunset and asks the reader to 'Don't forget me....I wasssss here" 
 Very well done!

From the Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler is a Newbery Medal-winning book with an unusual structure. Narrated by the 80-something-year-old Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler, this is the story of two kids who run away from home and live in New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. The New York classic art scene is enraptured by the discovered of what may be a new Michelangelo statue, a small marble carving of an angel. Who donated it? Why Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler, of course, and the story becomes a little mystery about the kids trying to figure out if it were a real Michelangelo. Along the way (i.e. in the last chapter) we learn who Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler is and there's a lot of exposition to clear everything up. 
 It's an interesting narrative conceit, having a book for young readers told by an old woman and structured with this strange frame story in which the book itself is actually a letter to the old woman's lawyer. The title only comes into play at the very end, and even then it's not particularly interesting or insightful or profound. If I'd read this book as a kid, I might have been confused (I was a slow-witted child), but as an adult I didn't find the story or the children particularly interesting. They mostly talk about how to budget their money on food and laundry and they complain about grammar a lot in what feels like a hamfisted attempt to make the book "educational." Their dialog is often Witty, with a capital W, specifically designed to come across as Witty. I also found the illustrations absolutely repulsive, especially an early one that shows the two kids mailing a letter and the brother's head isn't even the right shape and no human head can possibly angle that way and ew. 
 I can see a thread from this book to the myriad books for young readers that are about art mysteries, and even the Series of Unfortunate Events books, in which preternaturally intelligent young siblings solve mysteries together. I do have to admit that (small spoiler alert) I did enjoy when the kids in this book send the museum a letter claiming to have solved the mystery, and the museum basically responds, no shit we already figured that out. That felt realistic and true, and it kept the book from being a total one-star read for me. I also enjoyed Claudia's initial reasoning for running away, but I didn't feel that was explored much once she hightailed it out of Connecticut. 
 Having just read Harriet the Spy, I can't help but compare the two. I enjoyed Harriet because Harriet spied on others and told their stories. They were fascinating glimpses into the lives of a weird cross-section of people. In this book, all the characters seem to only think about themselves.

Solidly written twisted version of the Snow White story with a focus on the art of storytelling. Teachers and librarians could use this to teach upper elementary students about genre and have kids compare/contrast it to other versions of Snow White.

With Steve Rogers suddenly an old coot and retired, someone has to be Captain America: enter Cap's long-time sidekick, Sam Wilson aka the Falcon aka... the All-New Captain America! The Marvel version of Nazis, Hydra, are up to their old tricks and want to sterilise the human race with a blood bomb - it's up to Sam and his bird Redwing to save the world! 
 Hydra Ascendant sucks because Rick Remender's Captain America comics have always sucked. Whether he's writing Steve Rogers or Sam Wilson as Cap, he's the absolute pits only now he's trying to pass off a Falcon comic as a Captain America one. 
 What's worse is Sam is a completely useless replacement! Whether he's fighting a kid(!) or any one of Cap's rogues gallery from Batroc to Baron Zemo to Crossbones, Sam gets his ass handed to him up and down the street and needs someone like Nomad (Steve's son Ian from Remender's ghastly Castaway from Dimension Z storyline) or Misty Knight to save him! 
 The theme of the book is working together and the importance of community - that's why characters are always stepping in to help Sam - but either way he's not nearly competent enough to be Captain America. If I were a cynical soul (shut it!) I'd say Sam only got the gig because of positive discrimination... Nomad looks like a much better choice but then he's a white dude and wouldn't make headlines like a black Captain America would (and did). 
 The story is generic superhero twaddle (We gotta stop blah from blah end of the blah) but Remender's script is sloppy too - Redwing dies and comes back to life without any explanation, Sam can get stabbed straight through with a sword and appear to only be winded but the same thing happening to Baron Zemo puts him down, and the vampire dude wants to wipe out humanity even though he needs their blood to survive? Just garbage plotting! 
 Stuart Immonen's art is the only good thing about this comic. It's top-notch superhero artwork for a tossed-off script Remender clearly couldn't have cared less about. 
 The recent diversity changes at Marvel - female Thor, muslim Ms Marvel - have been great not because of these superficial changes but because Jason Aaron and G. Willow Wilson have written fantastic unique stories with these characters. Rick Remender's black Captain America is just an arbitrary change in a worthless, utterly boring story. No wonder Marvel quickly brought back the original to replace the Falcon!

Two Classic Books on the Damming of the Missouri Are Rereleased 
 Last year, while traveling down U.S. Highway 83 to research my next book, I spent a day at the Fort Berthold Reservation, N.D. At the Scout's Post No. 1, where those who served with Lt. Col. Custer at the Battle of Little Big Horn are interred, I met an Arikara man and Vietnam vet, Don Dickens. 
 Retired from the tribal government, he spends his free time taking care of the lonely graveyard. The remains of veterans from several wars there were once buried in the bottomlands along the Missouri River, but they were relocated when the flood came. 
 This inundation was not a spring runoff, but a manmade disaster created by two U.S. agencies, the Army Corps of Engineers and the Bureau of Reclamation. 
 Unlike most Native peoples, the Arikara, Mandan and Hidatsa had not been forced onto a reservation not of their choosing. They were sedentary peoples who had lived along the river for centuries. And then in the 1940s, Congress and the federal government, in response to devastating floods in downriver communities such as Omaha, pushed legislation through that created several projects to dam the Missouri and several of its tributaries. There's little evidence that any of these bureaucrats and legislators gave a second thought to the Native American communities that resided along the bottomlands. None were consulted prior to the law being enacted. Despite the belated protests of the Three Affiliated tribes and other nations up and downstream, the projects continued. 
 "It destroyed a way of life. Everybody farmed. Everybody had gardens and cattle. They ranched. They took it all away, and now they eat commodities. Everybody has developed diabetes and heart disease," Dickens told me. 
 Coincidentally, a few months after I visited the reservation, two important books chronicling this sad chapter of U.S. history were rereleased. 
 Dammed Indians Revisited: The Continuing History of the Pick-Sloan Plan and the Missouri River Sioux by Michael L. Lawson (South Dakota Historical Press) and Coyote Warrior: One Man, Three Tribes and the Trial That Forged a Nation by Paul VanDevelder (Bison Books), are two important works that together give a compete picture of how the tribes received the raw end of a deal they never asked for. 
 Both books take different approaches to the storytelling. Lawson is a historian and VanDevelder is a journalist. Dammed Indians Revisited deals primarily with the plight of the Lakotas who lived in the bottomlands along the Standing Rocking and Cheyenne River Reservations. Coyote Warrior is the story of the Three Affiliated Tribes. 
 Of the two books, I relate to VanDevelder's style the best. His story centers on the Cross family, who fought for justice for two generations. Martin Cross, a Hidatsa who married the daughter of Norwegian immigrants in the 1930s, was the first of his family to oppose the dam tooth and nail. Later, his son Raymond, an attorney specializing in federal Indian law, continued the fight to receive fair compensation for the tribes' losses. This character driven approach to writing history makes the story come alive for the reader. The relatively "dry" historical facts are interspersed with the narrative of this fascinating and tenacious family. 
 Dammed Indians Revisited is a more traditional history book, written by a trained historian. But what an incredible piece of work this is. It includes the best blow-by-blow account of how the Pick-Sloan plan came to be. (Raymond Cross figures in this work as well). 
 Some regard this book as a "classic," and I agree. Those who study the forcible removal of communities to make way for dams have been referring to it for years. First published in 1982, the new edition of this work is most welcome. It is almost a new book with several new chapters and detailed updates of events since 1980. New forewords from the author and former South Dakota Sen. George McGovern are included, along with the original written by Vine Deloria, Jr. Those who read the book in its first iteration, or libraries who have the first edition, will want to add this work to their collections. 
 The same can't be said for Coyote Warrior, which first came out in 2004. Except for a new afterword by the author, there isn't much new here. 
 However, these are not competing books, but complementary. They should be read together. And their near simultaneous rereleases should bring further attention to yet another sad chapter in the federal government's callous mistreatment of Native peoples. 
 Quoted in the new afterward in Coyote Warrior, Raymond Cross perhaps said it best: "This story is the retelling of the oldest story we have. It's story that goes back to the Greeks and before. It's the story of the struggle for justice, the struggle for dignity, and it's the story about the indomitability of the human spirit." 
 Stew Magnuson is the author of the award-winning nonfiction book, The Death of Raymond Yellow Thunder: And Other True Stories from the Nebraska-Pine Ridge Border Towns. He can be reached at www.stewmagnuson.com.

Satu kata untuk buku ini: EDHYAN!! 
 Saya takjub dengan isi dari buku ini. Mbah Sujiwo Tejo berhasil membuat saya hanyut dalam cinta "AKU" yang merasa dirinya sebagai "Wayang Rahwana". Ya, wayang. Karena bukan "Aku" yang menggerakkan cinta. 
 "Bahwa menikah itu nasib, mencintai itu takdir. Kamu dapat berencana menikah dengan siapa, tapi tak bisa kamu rencanakan cintamu untuk siapa... Bahwa yang membekas dari lilin itu bukan lelehnya, melainkan wajahmu sebelum gelap..." - Aku (Rahwana) 
 "Aku ingin mencintaimu walau penuh cacat, Rahwana. Tak peduli cacat itu membawa keburukan atau malah menampilkan hal yang indah-indah..." - Sinta 
 Menurut saya, inti dari buku ini tersirat pada makna Sastrajendra Hanyuningrat Pangruwating Diyu. Bahwa kegelapan melindungi seluruh warna. Kegelapan: Salah. Warna: Benar. 
 Berarti tak ada salah dan benar? Benar dan salah sama saja? 
 "Benar dan salah tentu ada. Tegakkanlah segitiga. Pada alas ada dua sudut, sudut benar dan sudut salah. Sinta, mari tarik lagi alas segitiga itu ke atas. Makin ke atas, sudut benar dan sudut salah itu semakin dekat. Di puncaknya, kedua sudut itu melenyap. Itulah titik Tuhan." - Aku (Rahwana) 
 "Salahkah Rahwana? Salahkah Sukesi? Aku selalu kurang tertarik untuk memikirkannya. Lebih suka aku untuk mencoba memahami semuanya, seperti Rahwana memahami dunia apa adanya melalui Sastrajendra Hanyuningrat Pangruwating Diyu. Ya, aku lebih tertarik untuk mencoba memahami." - Aku (Rahwana) 
 Memahami seisi dunia apa adanya. Memahami cinta. Jadi nikmati saja prosesnya, seperti saat menikmati jalan cerita yang absurd dalam buku ini ehehe. 
 Ohya, bagian favorit saya dalam buku ini adalah puisi terjemahan yang disisipkan oleh Mbah Tejo dalam bab 'Mata Sapi'.

Linked, by Imogen Howson, is a fascinating book with a captivating story line. 
 Elissa's discovery that she has a twin sister is shocking. But worse is the state she finds Lin in: bruised, battered, and terrified of the people who have held her captive for fifteen years. With no one left to trust, Elissa and Lin go on the run, change their looks and leave no trace behind - but still they're barely a step ahead of the agents who are hunting them. Because Elissa and Lin are too valuable to let go - and the dark truth at the heart of it all is too terrible to risk exposing... 
 This book isn't really what the blurb describes it as. In actuality, it's more sci-fi fantasy than expected and is more about the relationships between the characters and less about the actual escape (although that still plays a big role). However, that isn't to say it isn't a good book. On the contrary, I found this book very enjoyable and once I got to around half way, I just couldn't put it down and ended up finishing it in one night. 
 The relationship between Elissa and her twin/Spare, Lin, is such a complicated connection but it's the most realistic it could be in the fantastical situation playing out. At first, Elissa is weary of her twin and rightly so, this mysterious girl, who looks exactly like her, turns up out of the blue, the only indication of her existence being the bruises, migraines and hallucinations Lissa has been having for the past three years. But the girl lying there seemed worse off than her, so Lissa helped her. All the while, she's thinking that she doesn't trust her lookalike. At first, Lissa seemed right to trust the people around her, i.e. Her parents and not Lin and her twin seemed slightly crazy to trust no one but Lissa but when Lissa tells her parents about the girl she found, who had been causing her symptoms and that she looked exactly like her, their reaction was definitely the crazy one, not to mention learning about Lin's backstory made it impossible not feel sympathetic and give her free pass fro pretty much everything. From then, the real action of the book started, the girls went on the run and we get to see into how their relationship grows when it's just them. I personally, thought it was sweet that when Lin was worried or afraid Lissa would take her hand and help her through it, especially when it becomes obvious that Lin has almost zero experience with people and adding some hilarity, table manners and knowing she shouldn't kill people. As the book progressed, the link between the two sisters only strengthened and seemed to be a testament to the bond of twins, where as Lissa and Bruce's relationship seemed to be full of snarky comments and unsaid jealousy on Lissa's part; and their was no relationship between Lin and Bruce at all (this is not a surprise though, as never met). And in further comparison, the parental relationships Lissa has left much to be desired. The way the book described Lissa's mother, Mrs Ivory, made me really not like her. She is characterised as manipulative, uncaring, dismissive; especially of Lissa's symptoms and even at times unloving towards her daughter. I thought this was horrible and made me glad that Lissa left but when her mother is offered a way out at the end of the book (which I wont spoil) that felt really annoying. What made this worse is that she was perfectly civil towards, Bruce, her son, who's part of the SFI, a prestigious company employing the smartest people to fly spaceships. 
 Another relationship, definitely less complex than the one between Lissa and Lin, is between Caden and Lissa. Originally Caden thought she was a spoiled little girl whilst she was in love with him (although this was about 4 years before the book is set) and then as she expressed her distain during their flight (now during the book), he began to fall in love with her. I found it incredibly frustrating but also obvious from the start that they would end up together, perhaps because this is a YA novel or because it was the only pairing available for Lissa. But nonetheless I did enjoy them finally saying how they really feel. The only thing that really bothered me about Caden and Lissa is that when they said they loved each other and particularly Caden's confession, the feelings had only happened in the last few days. I found this more unrealistic than them being in space getting attacked by government space ships because of Lissa's electrokinetic twin. It's definitely not that I don't like them together; I just think a lot of YA novels have an unreasonable view on love. 
 Going back to the setting and the storyline of the book, I thought the setting up of the storyline was brilliant, it had a intricate backstory that may be a little bit confusing at the start but is interesting and soon makes a lot more sense. I also thought it was extremely clever of Imogen Howson to explain and describe a completely new world and new way of life within a few chapters. She managed to give Lissa a plausible but not piteous background and give life to the world of Sekoia, the SFI and what is later termed the IPL, all whilst being these chapters being set at a doctor's office. I also thought the relevance of this book, although written in 2013, is still prominent. People talking about what life could be like when Earth is done and will we move to space is an ever present question although not completely addressed in this book it is moved past as if it already has an answer which is an interesting take on the issue. I particularly enjoyed the chapters explaining how this way of life happened and found the justifications for why things were they were so interesting. 
 The only criticism I have of this book; is that I wish the blurb could be more accurate. I remember picking this book up from the bookstore thinking it wouldn't have anything to do with space as it isn't mentioned once on the back. Even though I was pleasantly surprised by the sci-fi themes, I was confused as to the setting for a while. 
 I would definitely recommend this book to everyone for any spare time you have. It is not a complicated book and does not have to be read with 100% concentration, however, once you start it, you may want to read it until it's finished. I give this book an 8/10

This is a book of truncations, though whether it's a cut-up or a hatchet piece is up to the reader. At the heart of this cobbled-together book is the issue of hero worship. Knight, confronted with circumstantial evidence that his guru/hero, Peter Lamborn Wilson (aka Hakim Bey), has some creepy enthusiasms, makes a point to publicly kill and dismember his Buddha in the road. Sadly, this derails a very engaging history of the unusual Moorish Orthodox Church of America (full disclosure- I belong to and helped found the Dallas branch) which gets ignored in its post-Wilson/Bey manifestations. Repeatedly, MOCA members are arrogantly dismissed as white pot-smoking fan-boys, and toward the end of the book, the MOCA gets lumped in with the one-joke-wonder Church of the Subgenius and played for laughs. The only insight a reader gets into the many distinct and interesting MOCA temples is the position of each interviewee on the Wilson-Bey accusations. This is tragic since the first wave history of the Church is given in great and interesting detail. The subsequent spread of the MOCA, its scholars and luminaries, the various traditions and accomplishments are all ignored. Instead the reader gets another truncation- a fragment of Knight's ultimate, unfinished Islamo-Queer science fiction novel, which is much less compelling than what preceded it. Then Knight plays cut-up with the Qu'ran for a bit. What we're left with is a hodge-podge unworthy of the promise of the first section. 
 I have read a wide variety of forbidden and controversial authors, including criminals, perverts, murderers, fascists, monsters, whores, politicians, and more. I value the intellectual freedom to consider what others dismiss out of hand. I do not think that such curiosity taints readers. Knight takes pains to depict his literary hatchet-piece as a personal betrayal from his guru for not living up to expectations. Wilson, like Henry Corbin, studied Persian philosophy in Iran under the Shah, admittedly a tyrant. Knight finds fault. The books grinds down as Knight vents his Death of 1,000 cuts on his hero and personal teacher. Ironically, the MOCA is anti-guru and offers a wealth of interesting material to those, unlike Knight, who eschew gurus and masters. This makes 'William S. Burroughs vs The Quran' an interesting case of missing the point. While much of the book is well written and meticulously researched, it is also incredibly selective and curiously incomplete. Our only solace is Knight's plunge into a kind of self-indulgent breakdown, making an impromptu mosque on his late father's remote property, cutting up the Qu'ran, per the Burroughs and Gysin cut-up method, and realizing- too late for the reader- that he, too, is no hero. Having completed literary assassination, Knight can't measure up to the writer he disowns or even complete the history he began. 
 In short, this is a sometimes interesting mess that collapses as Knight cuts,pastes, undermines, snipes, and fails utterly to consider the impact of various MOCA temples and lodges, each with its own romance and specialty. Make no mistake- this could have been a great book had Knight's obsessive vendetta been relegated to a footnote. Having torn down the statue of Ozymandias, Knight whiles away the balance of this book biting that idol's stone ankles and using old fragments for filler.
